questions.title: ROW_NUMBER vs. RANK vs. DENSE_RANK
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in SQL Server. If two products are tied for the highest price, what number does each function give the row right after them?
questions.modelAnswer: All three are ranking window functions used with OVER(ORDER BY ...), and all three number rows based on the order you specify, but they disagree on what happens with ties. ROW_NUMBER() always assigns a unique, sequential integer to every row, even when two rows are tied on the ORDER BY column -- one of the tied rows arbitrarily gets the lower number. RANK() gives tied rows the same number, but then skips ahead by the size of the tie: if two rows tie for rank 1, the next distinct row gets rank 3, not 2, because RANK() is really counting 'how many rows came before or tied with me, plus one.' DENSE_RANK() also gives tied rows the same number, but the next distinct value gets the very next integer with no gap -- it's counting distinct values, not rows. So for two products tied for the most expensive: ROW_NUMBER gives them 1 and 2 (arbitrarily), RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 3, and DENSE_RANK gives them both 1 and the next product gets 2.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it with a concrete example because the difference only shows up when there's a tie. Say I'm ranking products by ListPrice and two products are tied for the top price. ROW_NUMBER() doesn't know about ties at all -- it just hands out 1, 2, 3, 4 in order, so the two tied products arbitrarily get 1 and 2. RANK() respects the tie -- both get rank 1 -- but it still 'reserves' a slot for each of them, so the next product down is rank 3, not 2. DENSE_RANK() is the one that feels most natural for something like a pricing tier: both tied products get 1, and the next distinct price is simply 2, no gap. In practice I reach for ROW_NUMBER() constantly for deduplication -- partition by the natural key, order by something like an ID, and anything with RowNum greater than 1 is a duplicate I can delete. I reach for RANK() when ties should genuinely cost a position, like a sales leaderboard where two reps tied for 2nd really does mean nobody is 3rd. And I reach for DENSE_RANK() when I just want the next distinct tier number and don't want gaps confusing anyone reading the report.
questions.example:
SELECT Name, ListPrice,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RowNum,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS Rank_,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS DenseRank_
FROM Production.Product
ORDER BY ListPrice DESC;
-- If two products tie for the top ListPrice:
-- RowNum:     1, 2, 3, 4...  (ties broken arbitrarily)
-- Rank_:      1, 1, 3, 4...  (skips to 3 after the tie)
-- DenseRank_: 1, 1, 2, 3...  (no gap after the tie)
commonMistakes: Saying ROW_NUMBER() can produce duplicate numbers for ties (it never can -- it's always unique)
Mixing up which function skips numbers after a tie (it's RANK, not DENSE_RANK)
Forgetting that ROW_NUMBER() requires ORDER BY inside OVER() -- without it, row order is undefined
Not realizing all three still need PARTITION BY to restart numbering per group
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() always produces unique numbers, ties broken arbitrarily
RANK() gives ties the same number and skips ahead by the tie size afterward
DENSE_RANK() gives ties the same number with no gap for the next distinct value
Choice depends on whether the business question treats a tie as 'costing' a rank

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes ROW_NUMBER's uniqueness behavior
Correctly describes RANK's gap-after-tie behavior
Correctly describes DENSE_RANK's no-gap behavior
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over another

questions.title: Transactions: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
questions.prompt: Explain what a transaction is in SQL Server, what COMMIT does that running the statements without a transaction wouldn't, and what exactly ROLLBACK undoes.
questions.modelAnswer: A transaction groups one or more statements into a single all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION marks the start of that group. Until COMMIT runs, the changes are provisional -- visible in the current session but not yet permanently saved, and still subject to being undone. COMMIT TRANSACTION makes every change inside the group permanent, all at once. ROLLBACK TRANSACTION undoes every change made since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION, as if none of it had ever happened. The reason this matters: a multi-step change (like moving stock from one location to another with two separate UPDATE statements) can fail halfway through if run as two independent statements, leaving the data in an inconsistent state. Wrapping both statements in a transaction guarantees either both succeed or neither does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I usually explain this with the classic example: moving inventory from warehouse A to warehouse B is really two UPDATEs -- subtract from A, add to B. If I just run those as two separate statements and the second one fails, I've got stock that's vanished into nowhere. A transaction fixes that by treating both statements as one all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN TRANSACTION starts the clock; until I COMMIT, those changes are provisional -- I can see them in my own session, but they're not durably saved and SQL Server can still throw them away. COMMIT makes them permanent. ROLLBACK is the safety net -- if something goes wrong partway through, it undoes everything back to the BEGIN, cleanly, as if I'd never run anything at all. The discipline I bring to it professionally is keeping transactions as short as possible, because every lock held inside one is held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK runs.
commonMistakes: Thinking changes inside a transaction are already permanent before COMMIT runs
Forgetting that ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN TRANSACTION, not just the most recent statement
Leaving a transaction open for a long time, holding locks and blocking other users unnecessarily
Not pairing every BEGIN TRANSACTION with a guaranteed COMMIT or ROLLBACK, even on the error path
keyPoints: A transaction is an all-or-nothing group of statements
Changes are provisional until COMMIT makes them permanent
ROLLBACK undoes everything since the matching BEGIN TRANSACTION
Transactions exist to prevent partial, inconsistent multi-step changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what a transaction groups together
Correctly explains what COMMIT does and the provisional state before it
Correctly explains the scope of what ROLLBACK undoes
Gives a realistic scenario showing why this matters

questions.title: EXISTS vs. IN vs. JOIN for Existence Checks
questions.prompt: You need to find every customer who has placed at least one order. Compare writing this with EXISTS, with IN, and with an INNER JOIN plus DISTINCT. Explain how each one behaves when a customer has multiple orders, and the specific trap with NOT IN when the subquery's column can contain NULLs.
questions.modelAnswer: EXISTS, IN, and INNER JOIN with DISTINCT can all answer 'does this customer have at least one order,' but they get there differently. EXISTS(subquery) is a pure existence check -- SQL Server can stop scanning the moment it finds one matching row, and a customer with ten orders still only produces one result row, because EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's rows, just a true/false per outer row. IN (subquery) compares the outer column against the whole list the subquery returns; it also naturally avoids duplication since it's testing membership, not joining. An INNER JOIN behaves differently: joining Customer to Order on CustomerID and a customer with three orders produces three joined rows, which means DISTINCT (or GROUP BY) is required afterward to get back to one row per customer -- without it, the result silently overcounts. The sharper trap is with NOT IN rather than IN: if the subquery's column can contain a NULL, NOT IN against that list returns no rows at all for every single outer row, because SQL's three-valued logic can never prove an inequality against an unknown value. EXISTS doesn't have this problem because it's testing a condition, not comparing against a value list, which is one reason NOT EXISTS is generally the safer choice for 'does not have a match.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through why these three roads to the same destination aren't actually equivalent in practice. EXISTS is the one I reach for by default for a pure existence check -- it's a yes/no test, the optimizer can bail out the instant it finds one match, and a customer with ten orders still contributes exactly one row to the result, because EXISTS never pulls the subquery's actual data back. IN behaves similarly for this particular case -- it's checking membership in a list, not joining, so it also doesn't duplicate. Where people get burned is reaching for a plain INNER JOIN instead: the moment you join Customer to Order, a customer with three orders becomes three rows, and if you forget the DISTINCT, you've silently inflated your result set without an error anywhere to tell you. But the real gotcha I always bring up, because it's bitten people in production, is NOT IN with a nullable column -- if even one NULL sneaks into the subquery's result, NOT IN returns completely empty, for every row, with no warning. I treat that as a hard rule: never write NOT IN against a column that could contain NULL -- use NOT EXISTS instead, which doesn't have that failure mode at all.
questions.example:
-- EXISTS: pure existence check, no duplication risk
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM [Order] o WHERE o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID);

-- IN: membership test against the subquery's result list
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o);

-- JOIN: requires DISTINCT or a customer with 3 orders appears 3 times
SELECT DISTINCT c.CustomerID, c.Name
FROM Customer c
INNER JOIN [Order] o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID;

-- THE TRAP: if Order.CustomerID can be NULL, this returns ZERO rows for every customer:
SELECT c.CustomerID FROM Customer c
WHERE c.CustomerID NOT IN (SELECT o.CustomerID FROM [Order] o); -- avoid if nullable
commonMistakes: Writing a plain INNER JOIN for an existence check and forgetting DISTINCT, silently duplicating customers with multiple orders
Using NOT IN against a subquery column that can contain NULL, not realizing it returns zero rows for every outer row
Assuming EXISTS and IN always perform identically to a JOIN, when EXISTS can short-circuit and avoid materializing the whole list
Not recognizing that EXISTS never actually returns the subquery's column values -- only whether a match exists
keyPoints: EXISTS is a short-circuiting existence check; it returns one result row regardless of how many matches exist
IN compares against a list but doesn't duplicate rows the way a JOIN does
An INNER JOIN needs DISTINCT/GROUP BY to avoid duplicating a row per matching child record
NOT IN against a nullable column can return zero rows entirely -- NOT EXISTS avoids that trap

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains EXISTS's existence-check, non-duplicating behavior
Correctly explains why a JOIN needs DISTINCT to avoid duplication
Correctly identifies the NOT IN / NULL trap and why NOT EXISTS avoids it
Provides correct, illustrative SQL for at least two of the three approaches

questions.title: CTEs vs. Views: Same Shape, Different Lifetime
questions.prompt: A coworker says, "I don't get why we need views — a CTE already lets me name a subquery." Explain the real difference between a CTE and a view, and when you'd reach for one over the other.
questions.modelAnswer: A CTE and a view can look nearly identical — both let you name a SELECT and reference it like a table — but they differ in lifetime and scope. A CTE, defined with WITH, exists only for the single statement immediately following it; the moment that statement finishes, the CTE is gone, and no other query, session, or user can reference it. A view, created with CREATE VIEW, is a permanent database object: it's saved once and can be queried by name from any session, any user with permission, indefinitely, until someone runs DROP VIEW. Neither one stores actual data — both re-run their underlying SELECT against live data every time they're referenced. The practical rule: reach for a CTE to make one complex query more readable, especially when you need to reference the same intermediate result twice in that query. Reach for a view when the same logic needs to be reused across many different queries, by many different people or tools, including reporting tools like Power BI connecting directly to the database.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the one-sentence version first: a CTE lives for one statement, a view lives forever until someone deletes it. If I'm writing a gnarly query with three levels of nested subqueries and I just want to name the middle layer so I can read my own logic back, that's a CTE — it's disposable, scoped to right here, right now. But if I've built a 'active customers with more than $1,000 in lifetime orders' query that three different reports are going to need, I don't want three copies of that logic drifting out of sync — I'd save it once as a view, under a clear name, so every query and every person on the team references the same definition. I'd also mention that a view is a real object other tools can see too — if Power BI is connecting directly to the database instead of importing through Power Query, it can query a view exactly like a table, which a CTE could never support.
questions.example:
-- CTE: scoped to this one statement only
WITH RecentOrders AS (
    SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
    WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
    GROUP BY CustomerID
)
SELECT * FROM RecentOrders WHERE Total > 5000;
-- RecentOrders no longer exists after this statement runs.

-- View: saved permanently, reusable by anyone with access
CREATE VIEW vw_RecentOrderTotals AS
SELECT CustomerID, SUM(TotalDue) AS Total
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01'
GROUP BY CustomerID;

SELECT * FROM vw_RecentOrderTotals WHERE Total > 5000;
commonMistakes: Assuming a CTE can be reused across multiple separate statements or sessions (it can't)
Assuming either one stores a physical copy of the data (both re-run their SELECT live)
Reaching for a view for a one-off readability fix inside a single complex query, when a CTE is simpler and doesn't leave a permanent object behind
Forgetting that a view is directly queryable by reporting tools connecting to the database, the way a CTE never could be
keyPoints: A CTE is scoped to one statement; a view persists until explicitly dropped
Neither stores data — both run their SELECT fresh against live data each time
CTEs suit one-off readability inside a single complex query
Views suit logic that needs to be reused across many queries, people, or tools

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains a CTE's one-statement lifetime
Correctly explains a view's persistent, reusable lifetime
States that neither stores data, both re-run live
Gives a realistic scenario for choosing one over the other

questions.title: withColumn() vs. select() for Adding a Derived Column
questions.prompt: In PySpark, you need to add a new column to a DataFrame that's a tax-adjusted version of an existing Price column. Explain the difference between doing this with withColumn() and doing it with select(), and why calling withColumn() in a tight loop to add dozens of columns one at a time is a performance anti-pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: withColumn() adds or replaces exactly one named column while implicitly keeping every other column as-is -- it's the natural choice when you just need to bolt one derived value onto an otherwise unchanged DataFrame. select() instead requires you to explicitly list every column you want in the output, including the ones you're keeping unchanged, alongside the new expression -- more to type, but it makes the full resulting shape explicit in one line. The performance issue isn't withColumn() itself, it's calling it repeatedly in a loop: each call adds another Project node to Spark's logical plan, and chaining dozens of them one at a time builds a deeply nested plan that the Catalyst optimizer has to analyze, which can become genuinely slow (and in extreme cases has caused analysis errors) as the chain grows. The fix is building all the new column expressions up front and applying them together in a single select(), rather than looping withColumn() calls one column at a time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain withColumn() as the 'just this one column' tool -- call it once, give it a name and an expression, and everything else on the DataFrame passes through untouched. select() is the 'describe the whole output' tool -- I have to name every column I want, including ones I'm not changing, but in exchange I get a single line that says exactly what the result looks like. Where this actually matters in practice is when someone writes a for loop that calls withColumn() once per new column needed -- maybe 30 times -- because each one of those calls adds another layer to the query plan, and that nested plan gets genuinely expensive to analyze as it grows. I'd batch all 30 derived expressions into a list and apply them in one select() call instead, which produces the identical result with one pass through plan analysis instead of 30.
questions.example:
# Fine for a single derived column:
df2 = df.withColumn("PriceWithTax", col("Price") * 1.08)

# Equivalent, explicit full-shape version with select():
df2 = df.select("*", (col("Price") * 1.08).alias("PriceWithTax"))

# ANTI-PATTERN: looping withColumn() to add many columns one at a time
for new_col, expr in many_derived_columns.items():
    df = df.withColumn(new_col, expr)   # builds a deeply nested plan

# BETTER: batch all expressions into one select()
df = df.select("*", *[expr.alias(name) for name, expr in many_derived_columns.items()])
commonMistakes: Believing withColumn() always recomputes the whole DataFrame expensively, when the real cost is calling it repeatedly in a loop, not using it once
Not realizing select() requires explicitly naming every column you want to keep
Building 30+ sequential withColumn() calls in a loop instead of batching into one select()
Assuming the two approaches produce different results when used correctly for a single column add
keyPoints: withColumn() adds or replaces one named column while implicitly keeping all others
select() requires explicitly listing every column kept, but makes the full output shape explicit
Calling withColumn() repeatedly in a loop builds a deeply nested plan that slows analysis
The fix is batching many column expressions into a single select() call

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains withColumn()'s single-column add/replace behavior
Correctly explains select()'s explicit-column-list requirement
Correctly explains why looping withColumn() calls is a performance anti-pattern
Provides correct, relevant PySpark example code

questions.title: What MERGE actually does
questions.prompt: A coworker wants to sync a staging table into a permanent dimension table using separate UPDATE, INSERT, and DELETE statements. Explain what the MERGE statement does instead, and what each of its three WHEN clauses corresponds to.
questions.modelAnswer: MERGE combines insert, update, and delete logic into a single statement based on a join between a target table and a source. You join target and source ON some matching key, then handle three scenarios: WHEN MATCHED runs when a row exists in both target and source -- typically an UPDATE, equivalent to an INNER JOIN match. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET runs when a row exists in source but not target -- typically an INSERT, equivalent to the unmatched side of a LEFT JOIN from source. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE runs when a row exists in target but not source -- typically a DELETE (or an update to mark it inactive), equivalent to the unmatched side of a LEFT JOIN from target. All of this happens in one atomic statement instead of three separate ones with separate matching logic.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them MERGE is exactly the three statements they're already writing, just unified around one join so you don't have to repeat the matching logic three times and risk it drifting out of sync between statements. I always explain it by mapping it back to joins, because that's the mental model people already have: WHEN MATCHED is your INNER JOIN case -- the row is in both places, so update it. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET is the new rows showing up in the source that haven't landed in the target yet -- insert them. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE is rows that used to be in the target but have disappeared from the source -- that's your delete, or sometimes a soft-delete flag instead. For warehouse loads specifically, I like MERGE because the whole sync is one atomic operation -- there's no window where the target is left half-updated if something fails partway through.
questions.example:
MERGE Production.Product AS target
USING StagingProduct AS source
    ON target.ProductID = source.ProductID
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET target.ListPrice = source.ListPrice
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (ProductID, Name, ListPrice)
    VALUES (source.ProductID, source.Name, source.ListPrice)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN
    DELETE;
-- One atomic statement instead of three separate UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE statements.
commonMistakes: Confusing WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET (new rows to insert) with WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE (stale rows to delete)
Forgetting MERGE requires a semicolon terminator in SQL Server
Not realizing MERGE is still just a join under the hood -- overcomplicating the explanation
Using MERGE for a simple single-table update when a plain UPDATE would be simpler and clearer
keyPoints: MERGE unifies insert, update, and delete around one source-to-target join
WHEN MATCHED = INNER JOIN case (update)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET = new row in source (insert)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE = row missing from source (delete)
The whole sync happens in one atomic statement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what MERGE replaces and why it's useful
Correctly maps all three WHEN clauses to their scenarios
Connects the WHEN clauses to join semantics (INNER/LEFT JOIN unmatched sides)

questions.title: Completeness vs. Validity: Different Checks, Different Failures
questions.prompt: A coworker says a table 'passed data quality' because every required column is populated with no NULLs. Explain why that's a completeness check, not a validity check, and why a table can be 100% complete and still contain garbage data. Give a concrete SQL example of each kind of check against a Customer table.
questions.modelAnswer: Completeness and validity are two different dimensions that happen to get conflated because both sound like 'the data is fine.' Completeness asks only whether a value is present at all -- no NULLs, no blanks -- and a column can score 100% on that measure while every single value in it is nonsense, because completeness never looks at what the value actually contains. Validity asks whether the value that IS present actually conforms to an expected format, domain, or rule -- a real email address shape, a phone number with the right digit count, a date that's actually a calendar date. A Customer.Email column filled entirely with the literal string 'N/A' or 'test@test' is 100% complete and 0% valid at the same time, and a completeness check alone will never catch that, because it's checking for the absence of a value, not the correctness of one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I've seen this exact gap cause real confusion, because 'no NULLs' and 'looks right' feel like the same statement but they're measuring completely different things. Completeness is a presence check -- is there something in the cell at all -- and it will happily report 100% on a column that's full of placeholder garbage, because garbage isn't NULL, it's just wrong. Validity is the check that actually looks at the content: does this value match the shape I expect. I'd show it with two separate queries rather than one combined score, because collapsing them into a single 'data quality percentage' is exactly how this gets missed in the first place -- a stakeholder sees 98% and assumes it means 98% correct, when it might only mean 98% populated.
questions.example:
-- Completeness: are values present at all?
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS TotalRows,
    SUM(CASE WHEN Email IS NULL OR LTRIM(RTRIM(Email)) = '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS MissingEmail,
    SUM(CASE WHEN Phone IS NULL OR LTRIM(RTRIM(Phone)) = '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS MissingPhone
FROM Customer;

-- Validity: are the present values actually well-formed?
SELECT
    SUM(CASE WHEN Email IS NOT NULL AND Email NOT LIKE '%_@_%.__%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS InvalidEmailFormat,
    SUM(CASE WHEN Phone IS NOT NULL AND Phone NOT LIKE '[0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS InvalidPhoneFormat
FROM Customer;
commonMistakes: Treating a 100% completeness score as proof the data is actually correct
Collapsing completeness and validity into a single 'data quality score' that hides which dimension actually failed
Writing a validity check that only tests NOT NULL, which is really just completeness again under a different name
Assuming a placeholder value like 'N/A' or 'test@test' will be caught by a completeness check (it won't -- it isn't NULL)
keyPoints: Completeness measures presence of a value; validity measures whether the present value is well-formed
A column can be 100% complete and still contain entirely invalid, garbage values
Validity checks need to test the actual content against a format/domain rule, not just NOT NULL
Reporting the two dimensions separately prevents a high completeness score from masking a validity problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes completeness from validity as separate dimensions
Explains concretely why 100% completeness doesn't imply correctness
Provides a correct, distinct SQL example for each check
Notes the risk of collapsing both into a single score

questions.title: Why a Clean Uniqueness Check Can Still Miss Duplicates
questions.prompt: A SQL uniqueness check on CustomerID shows zero duplicates. Finance insists there are duplicate customers in the system anyway. Explain how both of these can be true at the same time, and what kind of check would actually catch what finance is describing.
questions.modelAnswer: Both statements can be true because they're testing uniqueness at different levels. A SQL uniqueness check on CustomerID is a structural check: it verifies that the key column itself has no repeated values, which it will almost always pass, since CustomerID is usually a surrogate key generated to be unique by design. What finance is describing is a semantic duplicate -- the same real-world person represented by two different CustomerIDs, usually because they were entered twice through different channels, with slightly different spellings, typos, or formatting ('John Smith' vs. 'Jon Smith', same address). A structural uniqueness check on the key column has no way to see this, because from the database's point of view, those are two perfectly valid, unique rows. Catching this requires a different kind of check entirely: matching logic that compares normalized identifying attributes across rows -- name, address, phone, email -- to surface candidate duplicates that share the same real-world identity despite having different keys, which is the core concern of Master Data Management's deduplication and matching discipline, not a plain uniqueness constraint.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of those moments where the SQL check is technically doing exactly what it was asked to do, and the person asking for it actually wanted something different. A uniqueness check on CustomerID is really just confirming the primary key is doing its job -- no row shares another row's key -- which, on a surrogate key column, is basically guaranteed and not telling you anything meaningful about the real-world data. What finance is actually flagging is that the same human being has two separate rows, two separate CustomerIDs, probably because they signed up once through the web form and once through a call center, and a typo or formatting difference meant nobody caught it. That's a fuzzy-matching problem, not a key-constraint problem -- I'd need to normalize names and addresses (strip punctuation, standardize case, maybe soundex on last name) and look for rows that are suspiciously similar on those attributes despite having different keys, which is a genuinely different kind of query than anything a uniqueness check does.
commonMistakes: Assuming a passing uniqueness check on the primary key means there are no duplicate customers at all
Not distinguishing structural uniqueness (the key) from semantic/entity-level duplication (the real-world person)
Trying to fix this by adding more constraints to the key column, which can't detect a fuzzy match problem
Treating this as a one-off query instead of recognizing it as the entry point into MDM matching and deduplication
keyPoints: A uniqueness check on a surrogate key only verifies structural uniqueness of that column
Finance's complaint describes semantic/entity duplication -- the same real-world person under two different keys
Catching semantic duplicates requires matching logic on normalized identifying attributes, not a key constraint
This is fundamentally an MDM matching/deduplication problem, not a SQL uniqueness problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why both statements can be simultaneously true
Correctly distinguishes structural key uniqueness from semantic/entity duplication
Describes a concrete approach (normalized attribute matching) that would catch the real issue
Connects the problem to MDM matching/deduplication as the right discipline

questions.title: Business Glossary Term vs. Data Dictionary Entry
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between a business glossary term and a data dictionary entry for the same concept, like 'Active Customer'? Why do organizations need both instead of just picking one?
questions.modelAnswer: A business glossary term captures business meaning, independent of any specific system: 'Active Customer' as a glossary entry means something like 'a customer with at least one completed purchase in the trailing 12 months,' written in plain business language, owned by a business steward, with no reference to a specific table or column. A data dictionary entry is technical documentation of an actual physical implementation: the Customers.IsActive bit column, its data type, nullability, and the literal table it lives in. The two serve different purposes and can legitimately diverge: a system's IsActive flag might actually be set by a completely different rule than the glossary's stated definition, and without both documented, nobody can tell whether the technical implementation genuinely matches the intended business meaning. Organizations need both because the glossary gives a shared, system-independent vocabulary the business can agree on, while the dictionary documents what each system's engineers actually built -- and reconciling the two is often where real data quality issues surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as two different audiences asking two different questions about the same word. The business side asks 'what do we mean by Active Customer' -- that's the glossary's job, a plain-language definition that doesn't care which database or column implements it, and it's owned by someone in the business, not IT. The technical side asks 'where does this actually live and how is it typed' -- that's the dictionary's job, documenting the real column, its data type, whether it allows NULLs, which table it's in. The reason you can't just pick one: if you only have the dictionary, you know exactly what IsActive is as a column, but you have no idea whether the logic that sets it actually matches what the business thinks 'active' means. If you only have the glossary, you have a clean definition everyone agrees on, but no way to trace it to what's actually running in production. I've seen the gap between the two be exactly where a reported number quietly stops meaning what everyone assumes it means.
commonMistakes: Treating the glossary and the dictionary as redundant, documenting the same thing twice
Writing a dictionary entry that just restates the business definition instead of describing the physical column
Not checking whether a column's actual implementation logic genuinely matches its linked glossary term's definition
Letting only engineers own glossary terms, missing the business perspective the glossary exists to capture
keyPoints: A glossary term defines business meaning, independent of any specific system or column
A dictionary entry documents a specific physical implementation: table, column, data type, nullability
The two can diverge, and reconciling them is often where real data quality gaps are found
Both are needed: shared business meaning plus accurate technical documentation of how it's actually built

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a business glossary term's purpose and scope
Correctly defines a data dictionary entry's purpose and scope
Explains why the two can diverge and why that matters
Explains why an organization needs both rather than just one

questions.title: Column-Level vs. Table-Level Lineage
questions.prompt: Your lineage tool shows that a 'Revenue' report table is downstream of five source tables, but a developer asks specifically which source column feeds the 'NetRevenue' figure shown on the report. Explain the difference between table-level and column-level lineage, and why table-level lineage can't answer the developer's question.
questions.modelAnswer: Table-level lineage captures dependencies at the dataset level: it tells you 'Table A feeds Table B,' as a single edge in a graph, without distinguishing which specific columns in A contributed to which specific columns in B. Column-level lineage tracks that relationship at the individual field level, following a specific column's transformation path -- joins, filters, calculations -- across every hop from source to destination. The developer's question ('which source column feeds NetRevenue specifically') is a column-level question, and table-level lineage structurally cannot answer it, because it deliberately aggregates every column relationship between two tables into one coarse edge -- knowing that Table A feeds Table B tells you nothing about which of Table A's twenty columns actually matters for this one figure. Answering the real question requires either lineage tooling that parses the transformation logic at column granularity, or manually tracing the actual SQL/ETL code that builds NetRevenue.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the difference with exactly the gap in this question: table-level lineage is a map of 'these datasets are connected,' and that's genuinely useful for a broad picture of data flow, but it's the wrong altitude for the question actually being asked. The developer doesn't want to know that five tables generally feed the report -- they want to know the one specific source field that NetRevenue traces back to, through whatever joins and calculations sit in between. Table-level lineage can't give that because it was never tracking at that resolution in the first place -- it's like asking which specific word in five books inspired a sentence, when all you've recorded is which books someone read. Getting the real answer means either using a lineage tool that actually parses column-level transformations (which not every tool or every connector supports equally well), or going and reading the actual ETL/SQL logic by hand to trace it myself.
commonMistakes: Assuming table-level lineage implicitly contains column-level detail just because the tables are connected
Not recognizing that table-level lineage aggregates every column relationship into one coarse edge
Promising a column-level answer from a tool that only captures table-level lineage
Forgetting that manually tracing the actual transformation code is a valid fallback when column-level tooling isn't available
keyPoints: Table-level lineage tracks dataset-to-dataset dependencies, with no column granularity
Column-level lineage follows an individual field's transformation path across every hop
Table-level lineage structurally cannot answer which specific source column feeds a specific destination column
Column-level tooling or manual code tracing is required to answer a field-specific lineage question

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines table-level lineage and its granularity
Correctly defines column-level lineage and its granularity
Correctly explains why table-level lineage can't answer the developer's question
Mentions a realistic path to actually getting the column-level answer

questions.title: Golden Records and Survivorship Rules
questions.prompt: In Master Data Management, what is a 'golden record,' and when two source systems disagree about the same customer's address, how does a survivorship rule decide which value wins? Give a concrete example of a survivorship rule.
questions.modelAnswer: A golden record is the single, trusted, consolidated version of a master data entity -- a customer, a product -- assembled from matched records across multiple source systems, meant to be the one authoritative version the rest of the enterprise can rely on instead of each system's own, possibly conflicting, copy. When two sources disagree about an attribute like address, a survivorship rule is the predefined, explicit logic that decides which source's value becomes part of the golden record for that specific attribute -- it exists precisely because simply trusting one source for every attribute is rarely correct, since different systems are often more reliable for different fields. A concrete example: 'most recently updated value wins' -- if a customer's address was last changed in the CRM two years ago but updated in the e-commerce platform's checkout flow last month, the survivorship rule picks the e-commerce platform's more recent value as the one that survives into the golden record.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd define a golden record as the answer to the question 'if I could only trust one version of this customer across the whole company, what would it look like' -- it's built by matching records that represent the same real entity across systems and then merging them into one consolidated, trusted version. The reason survivorship rules exist at all is that merging isn't as simple as picking a winning system once and sticking with it for every field, because no single system is the best source for everything. A rule I'd actually use: for address specifically, go with whichever source has the most recent update timestamp, since an address genuinely changes over time and recency is a reasonable proxy for accuracy there. But I'd pair that with a different rule for a different field -- say, always trust the ERP for billing address specifically, regardless of recency, because that's the system of record for anything tied to invoicing. The rules have to be field-specific and deliberate, not one blanket policy applied to the whole record.
commonMistakes: Defining a golden record as simply 'the most complete record' without mentioning it comes from matching and consolidating multiple sources
Assuming one source system should always win for every attribute, instead of per-field survivorship rules
Not giving a concrete, specific survivorship rule when asked, staying at a vague conceptual level
Confusing survivorship rules (which value wins) with matching rules (which records represent the same entity)
keyPoints: A golden record is the single trusted, consolidated version of an entity assembled from matched source records
Survivorship rules decide which source's value wins per attribute when sources disagree
Different attributes often need different survivorship logic, not one blanket rule
'Most recently updated wins' and 'a designated system of record wins for this field' are both common patterns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what a golden record is and how it's formed
Correctly explains what a survivorship rule decides and why it's needed
Gives a concrete, specific survivorship rule example
Recognizes different attributes may need different survivorship logic

questions.title: PII vs. Sensitive/Confidential Data
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between PII (personally identifiable information) and the broader category of 'sensitive' or 'confidential' data in a classification scheme. Give an example of a confidential data element that is not PII.
questions.modelAnswer: PII is data that can identify a specific individual, either directly (a name, a Social Security number) or indirectly when combined with other attributes (a date of birth plus a zip code plus a gender can narrow down to one specific person). Sensitive or confidential data is a broader category in most classification schemes, covering anything that would cause meaningful harm -- financial, competitive, legal, reputational -- if disclosed or misused, whether or not it's tied to an individual's identity at all. PII is a subset of that broader category, not a synonym for it. A concrete example of confidential-but-not-PII: a company's unreleased quarterly earnings figures before public disclosure -- leaking them could enable insider trading or cause real competitive and legal harm, but the data itself has no connection to any individual person's identity. A classification scheme that only has a 'PII' category and nothing broader leaves data like this, along with trade secrets and proprietary pricing models, effectively unclassified and unprotected.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct the common shorthand where people use 'sensitive' and 'PII' interchangeably, because they're not the same category and conflating them leaves real gaps in a classification scheme. PII specifically means it can be traced back to an individual -- a name, an SSN, or a combination of quasi-identifiers that narrows it down to one person. Sensitive or confidential is a bigger bucket: it's about the consequence of exposure, not about whose identity is attached. The example I'd give every time is unreleased financial results -- if next quarter's earnings numbers leak before the public announcement, that's a serious problem, potential insider trading exposure, competitive disadvantage, maybe even legal liability -- and none of that has anything to do with an individual person's privacy. If a classification scheme only has a PII bucket, that earnings data has nowhere to go and ends up unlabeled, which in practice means unprotected, because nobody applied the access controls that a confidential label would have triggered.
commonMistakes: Using 'PII' and 'sensitive/confidential' as if they're interchangeable terms for the same thing
Forgetting that indirect identifiers (combinations of quasi-identifiers) can also make data PII, not just direct identifiers
Not providing a genuine example of confidential-but-not-PII data when asked
Assuming a classification scheme without a broader 'confidential' category still adequately protects non-personal sensitive data
keyPoints: PII specifically identifies an individual, directly or through a combination of indirect identifiers
Sensitive/confidential is a broader category based on harm from disclosure, not tied to personal identity
PII is a subset of the broader sensitive/confidential category, not a synonym for it
Non-personal data (trade secrets, unreleased financials, pricing models) can be highly confidential without being PII

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines PII, including indirect identification
Correctly defines the broader sensitive/confidential category
Provides a genuine, specific confidential-but-not-PII example
Explains the practical risk of conflating the two categories

questions.title: Data Map vs. Data Catalog in Microsoft Purview
questions.prompt: In Microsoft Purview, what's the actual difference between the Data Map and the Data Catalog, and why does scanning a source populate one before the other becomes useful?
questions.modelAnswer: The Data Map is the underlying metadata repository -- the graph that stores the technical metadata Purview discovers about registered sources: assets, schemas, classifications, and lineage relationships, all built up by running scans against those sources. The Data Catalog is the curated, business-facing layer built on top of the Data Map, where that raw technical metadata gets enriched with business context -- glossary term links, descriptions, designated owners, data products -- so that a business user can actually search for and understand an asset, not just see its raw scanned schema. Scanning populates the Data Map first because scanning is literally the mechanism by which Purview discovers and registers an asset's technical metadata in the first place; the Catalog has nothing meaningful to curate until there's something in the Map to attach glossary terms, descriptions, and ownership to.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the Data Map as the plumbing and the Catalog as the room people actually walk into. The Map is where all the raw technical metadata lives -- what tables and columns exist, what data types they are, what classifications were detected, how things connect -- and it gets built up purely by scanning registered sources; nobody hand-types that layer. The Catalog is what a business user actually interacts with: search, browse by business domain, see a clear description and an owner's name, see which glossary term this asset maps to. Scanning has to come first because the Catalog's value entirely depends on there being real assets with real metadata to curate -- you can't write a helpful description and assign a steward to an asset that Purview doesn't know exists yet. In practice this means rolling out Purview well isn't 'turn on scanning and you're done' -- the scan is step one, and the curation work that makes the Catalog actually useful is a separate, ongoing effort on top of it.
commonMistakes: Treating the Data Map and the Data Catalog as the same thing or interchangeable terms
Assuming a completed scan alone produces a usable, business-friendly catalog without curation
Forgetting that classifications and lineage relationships live in the Data Map, discovered via scanning
Not explaining why curation (glossary links, descriptions, owners) has to happen after scanning, not instead of it
keyPoints: The Data Map is the technical metadata repository built by scanning registered sources
The Data Catalog is the curated, business-facing layer built on top of the Data Map
Scanning discovers and registers raw technical metadata; it doesn't add business context on its own
The Catalog only becomes useful once there's something in the Map to curate with descriptions, owners, and glossary links

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what the Data Map is and how it's populated
Correctly defines what the Data Catalog is and how it differs from the Map
Correctly explains why scanning must happen before curation is useful
Response is specific to Purview rather than a generic catalog description

questions.title: Top-2-per-group with a window function
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012's Production.Product table that returns the two highest-priced products in each color, without using a correlated subquery.
questions.modelAnswer: The idiomatic way to solve 'top N per group' in T-SQL is PARTITION BY plus ROW_NUMBER(), wrapped in a CTE so the ranking column can be filtered afterward. PARTITION BY Color restarts the numbering at 1 for each color, and ORDER BY ListPrice DESC makes 1 the most expensive product in that color. You can't filter directly on ROW_NUMBER() in the same SELECT's WHERE clause because window functions are logically evaluated after WHERE -- that's why the CTE (or a subquery) is necessary.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic 'top N per group' problem, and the pattern I reach for every time is a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by the grouping column. I avoid a correlated subquery with TOP 2 inside it because that approach re-executes once per outer row and doesn't scale well. Instead, I compute the rank once in a CTE, then just filter WHERE RankInColor <= 2 in the outer query. The one gotcha I always mention out loud in an interview: you cannot write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 2 directly in the same SELECT, because the WHERE clause is logically evaluated before window functions are computed -- that's exactly why the CTE wrapper is required, not just a style preference.
questions.example:
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Color ORDER BY ListPrice DESC) AS RankInColor
    FROM Production.Product
)
SELECT Name, Color, ListPrice
FROM Ranked
WHERE RankInColor <= 2
ORDER BY Color, RankInColor;
-- The CTE is required because ROW_NUMBER() can't be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE clause.
commonMistakes: Trying to filter WHERE ROW_NUMBER() <= 2 directly in the same SELECT (not legal -- window functions evaluate after WHERE)
Forgetting PARTITION BY and ranking across the whole table instead of per color
Using TOP 2 with a correlated subquery per group, which is correct but far less efficient on large tables
Omitting ORDER BY inside OVER(), which leaves 'top' undefined
keyPoints: PARTITION BY restarts the ranking per group (per color here)
A CTE or subquery is required to filter on the window function's result
ORDER BY DESC inside OVER() makes rank 1 the highest price
This pattern generalizes to any 'top N per group' business question

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses ROW_NUMBER() with correct PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
Wraps it in a CTE/subquery to filter correctly
Query is syntactically valid and returns exactly 2 rows per color
Explains why filtering can't happen in the same SELECT's WHERE clause

questions.title: Raising a custom business-rule error
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL that checks whether a discount percentage exceeds 50% and, if so, raises a custom error using the modern recommended syntax. Then show how you would log an error inside a CATCH block and still let it propagate to the caller.
questions.modelAnswer: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error, taking an error number, a message, and a state, and raising it exactly as if SQL Server had generated it itself. For a business rule like a discount cap, you check the condition and THROW a custom error if it's violated. To log an error and still propagate it, use THROW with no arguments inside a CATCH block -- it re-raises the exact error that was just caught, unmodified, after whatever logging or cleanup logic runs first. RAISERROR is the older syntax, still common in existing code, with a different argument shape (message, severity, state) -- recognize it, but prefer THROW for new code.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the business rule check itself, I'd write a simple IF that tests the discount, and THROW a custom error number with a clear message if it's violated -- that's the modern, recommended way, and it's a one-liner. The more interesting half of this question is re-throwing from a CATCH block, because that's a pattern people often get wrong: they either swallow the error silently after logging it, or they try to reconstruct it with a new THROW statement and lose the original error details. The clean way is TRY/CATCH around the risky operation, log whatever you need to inside CATCH, and then just write THROW with no arguments -- that re-raises the exact error that was caught, unmodified, so the caller still sees the real failure instead of a sanitized stand-in.
questions.example:
-- Business rule check
IF @DiscountPercent > 50
    THROW 50000, 'Discount cannot exceed 50 percent.', 1;

-- Logging then re-throwing the original error
BEGIN TRY
    UPDATE Sales.SpecialOffer SET DiscountPct = @DiscountPercent WHERE SpecialOfferID = @ID;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    INSERT INTO ErrorLog (ErrorMessage, LoggedAt) VALUES (ERROR_MESSAGE(), GETDATE());
    THROW; -- re-raises the exact caught error, unmodified
END CATCH
commonMistakes: Using RAISERROR for new code instead of the modern, recommended THROW
Writing a new THROW statement inside CATCH instead of bare THROW, which loses the original error's details
Forgetting THROW's argument order is (error number, message, state) -- a different shape than RAISERROR's
Swallowing the error entirely after logging it, instead of re-throwing so the caller knows it failed
keyPoints: THROW is the modern, recommended way to raise a custom error
Bare THROW inside CATCH re-raises the exact original error
RAISERROR is the older syntax, still seen in legacy code
Logging an error doesn't have to mean swallowing it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses THROW to raise a custom business-rule error
Correctly uses TRY/CATCH with bare THROW to re-raise after logging
Explains the difference between THROW and RAISERROR
Code is syntactically valid T-SQL

questions.title: Join Four Tables, Mixing INNER and LEFT
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012 that returns each order line's product name, order date, and the customer's first and last name, including order lines for products that may no longer have a subcategory assigned. Use at least one LEFT JOIN alongside INNER JOINs.
questions.modelAnswer: This requires chaining four tables together: SalesOrderHeader (for the order date and customer link), SalesOrderDetail (the order lines), Product (for the product name), and Person (for the customer's name), while also reaching ProductSubcategory with a LEFT JOIN so that products missing a subcategory still appear instead of being silently excluded. Each JOIN connects to whatever table already has the needed column available, not necessarily the very first table named in FROM — for instance, the join to Product uses ProductID from SalesOrderDetail, introduced by the join just before it. The LEFT JOIN to ProductSubcategory is the one deliberate choice: an INNER JOIN there would drop any order line whose product has a NULL ProductSubcategoryID, which is exactly the scenario the question asks to preserve.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this one join at a time rather than writing the whole thing at once, because that's the only way to keep four tables straight. I start from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail joined on SalesOrderID, since that's the backbone of the query. Then I bring in Product on ProductID to get the product name, and Person on CustomerID (really BusinessEntityID) to get the name. All three of those are INNER JOINs because I genuinely need a match on all of them for the row to make sense. The one place I'd stop and think is ProductSubcategory — the question specifically says some products might not have one, and an INNER JOIN there would quietly drop those order lines from the result with no warning. That's exactly the signal to use LEFT JOIN instead, so a product with a NULL ProductSubcategoryID still shows up, just with NULL in the subcategory column rather than vanishing from the report entirely.
questions.example:
SELECT soh.OrderDate, p.Name AS ProductName, per.FirstName, per.LastName, ps.Name AS SubcategoryName
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader AS soh
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON soh.SalesOrderID = sod.SalesOrderID
INNER JOIN Production.Product AS p
    ON sod.ProductID = p.ProductID
INNER JOIN Person.Person AS per
    ON soh.CustomerID = per.BusinessEntityID
LEFT JOIN Production.ProductSubcategory AS ps
    ON p.ProductSubcategoryID = ps.ProductSubcategoryID;
commonMistakes: Using INNER JOIN on ProductSubcategory, which silently drops any order line for a product missing a subcategory
Joining to the wrong table's column (e.g. trying to reach ProductID directly from SalesOrderHeader, which doesn't have it)
Forgetting table aliases on a four-table query, making it unreadable and error-prone to debug
Not noticing that CustomerID on SalesOrderHeader maps to BusinessEntityID on Person.Person, not a column literally named CustomerID there
keyPoints: Each JOIN can reference any table already available earlier in the query, not just the first one
LEFT JOIN preserves rows that would otherwise be dropped by a stricter INNER JOIN
Mixing INNER and LEFT JOIN in one query is normal when different relationships have different guarantees
Clear aliases are essential once a query joins more than two or three tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly joins all four required tables
Uses LEFT JOIN specifically for ProductSubcategory
Query is syntactically valid and returns the correct columns
Explains why LEFT JOIN was chosen there instead of INNER JOIN

questions.title: Writing a groupBy/agg Aggregation in PySpark
questions.prompt: Write a PySpark transformation against a DataFrame named orders (columns: region, order_id, amount) that returns, for each region, the total amount and the count of orders, sorted by total amount descending.
questions.modelAnswer: groupBy("region") groups the rows by region, and .agg() lets you compute multiple aggregates in a single pass over the grouped data -- sum("amount").alias("total_amount") and count("order_id").alias("order_count"). Since groupBy/agg returns a new, unsorted DataFrame, .orderBy(col("total_amount").desc()) is needed afterward to get the descending order the question asks for. All of this builds a single lazy transformation plan; nothing actually executes until an action like .show() or .write() triggers it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as one chain: group by region first, then agg() with both aggregates computed together rather than two separate groupBy calls, since agg() is built to take multiple aggregate expressions at once. I always import sum and count from pyspark.sql.functions with an alias (like _sum) so I don't accidentally shadow Python's own built-in sum and count, which is a subtle bug that's bitten people before. After the aggregation I chain orderBy with .desc() on the new total_amount column, because groupBy/agg's output isn't sorted by default -- people sometimes assume it comes back sorted by the aggregate just because that's what they asked for conceptually, but it's not, you have to ask for it explicitly.
questions.example:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as _sum, count, col

result = (orders
    .groupBy("region")
    .agg(
        _sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
        count("order_id").alias("order_count")
    )
    .orderBy(col("total_amount").desc()))
commonMistakes: Shadowing Python's built-in sum/count by importing them without aliasing the pyspark.sql.functions versions
Using count("amount") when amount could be null, undercounting rows with a null amount instead of using count("*") or count(lit(1))
Forgetting agg() can compute multiple aggregates in one call instead of chaining multiple separate groupBy calls
Calling .show() before .orderBy(), assuming groupBy's output is already sorted by default
keyPoints: groupBy(column) groups rows; agg() computes one or more aggregates per group in a single pass
Aliasing aggregate functions from pyspark.sql.functions avoids shadowing Python built-ins
orderBy sorts the resulting aggregated DataFrame, which isn't sorted by default
The whole chain is a lazy transformation until an action triggers execution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses groupBy with the right column
Correctly computes both aggregates in agg()
Correctly sorts descending by total amount
Avoids the built-in-shadowing/null-counting pitfalls

questions.title: Deduplicating to the Latest Record Per Key
questions.prompt: A bronze table customer_updates has multiple rows per customer_id, each with a different updated_at timestamp, because every change was appended rather than updated in place. Write PySpark code that keeps only the single most recent row per customer_id.
questions.modelAnswer: The standard pattern is a Window partitioned by customer_id, ordered by updated_at descending, with row_number() assigning 1 to the most recent row per partition, then filtering to row number == 1. dropDuplicates(["customer_id"]) is explicitly the wrong tool here because it keeps an arbitrary row per key, not necessarily the most recent one -- it has no concept of 'most recent,' only 'first encountered.'
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic dedup-to-latest pattern, and I'd reach for a Window every time rather than dropDuplicates, specifically because dropDuplicates has no idea which row is newest -- it just keeps whichever one it happens to encounter first, which isn't a guarantee of recency at all. I'd partition the window by customer_id, order by updated_at descending so the newest row in each partition gets rank 1, add that as a helper column with row_number(), filter down to rn == 1, and then drop the helper column before handing the result off. The one thing I always double check is the sort direction -- ordering ascending instead of descending by mistake silently keeps the oldest row instead of the newest, and nothing about the output looks obviously wrong unless you know to check for it.
questions.example:
from pyspark.sql import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import row_number, col

w = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(col("updated_at").desc())

latest = (customer_updates
    .withColumn("rn", row_number().over(w))
    .filter(col("rn") == 1)
    .drop("rn"))
commonMistakes: Using dropDuplicates(["customer_id"]) and assuming it keeps the most recent row (it keeps an arbitrary one)
Forgetting to order the window descending by updated_at, keeping the oldest row instead of the newest
Not dropping the helper rn column, leaving it in the final output
Using rank() instead of row_number(), which can return more than one row per customer if two updates share an identical timestamp
keyPoints: A Window partitioned by the key and ordered by the timestamp is the right dedup tool when 'most recent' matters
dropDuplicates has no sense of recency -- it keeps an arbitrary row per key
row_number() guarantees exactly one row per partition after filtering to rn == 1
The helper ranking column should be dropped from the final result

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly constructs the Window with the right partition/order
Correctly applies row_number() and filters to 1
Explains why dropDuplicates is the wrong tool here
Code is syntactically valid and drops the helper column

questions.title: Write a MERGE to sync a staging table into a dimension
questions.prompt: Write a MERGE statement that syncs a StagingCustomer table into a DimCustomer table: update existing customers' names, insert new customers, and leave customers who disappeared from staging alone (do not delete them).
questions.modelAnswer: This requires only two of MERGE's three WHEN clauses -- WHEN MATCHED for updates and WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET for inserts -- and deliberately omitting WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE, since the requirement is to leave disappeared customers untouched rather than deleting them. Omitting a WHEN clause simply means MERGE does nothing for that scenario.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key thing here is recognizing that MERGE's three WHEN clauses are each optional -- you only write the ones you need. Since the requirement explicitly says not to delete customers who vanish from staging, I just don't write a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause at all. MERGE doesn't require all three; leaving one out means that scenario simply does nothing, which is exactly the 'leave them alone' behavior requested. This comes up constantly in dimension loads -- you often want to sync new and changed records without ever purging history just because a source feed temporarily dropped a row.
questions.example:
MERGE DimCustomer AS target
USING StagingCustomer AS source
    ON target.CustomerID = source.CustomerID
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET target.CustomerName = source.CustomerName
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (CustomerID, CustomerName)
    VALUES (source.CustomerID, source.CustomerName);
-- No WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause -- customers missing from staging are left untouched.
commonMistakes: Adding a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE clause when the requirement explicitly says not to delete
Forgetting the trailing semicolon, which SQL Server requires after MERGE
Updating columns that didn't change, instead of only the ones the requirement calls for (CustomerName)
Joining on the wrong key (e.g. a surrogate key that doesn't exist yet in staging) instead of the natural/business key
keyPoints: WHEN clauses in MERGE are each optional -- omit the ones you don't need
Omitting WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE means disappeared rows are left alone, not deleted
Join on the business/natural key that staging and the dimension share
MERGE still requires a terminating semicolon in SQL Server

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct WHEN MATCHED update logic
Correct WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET insert logic
Correctly omits any delete logic per the requirement
Valid, runnable MERGE syntax with correct join predicate

questions.title: Writing SQL Completeness and Validity Checks
questions.prompt: Write SQL against a Customers table (columns: CustomerID, Email, Phone, SignupDate) that reports, for each of Email and Phone: the count and percentage of NULL/blank values (completeness), and the count of non-null values that fail a basic format check (validity) -- Email must contain '@', Phone must be exactly 10 digits.
questions.modelAnswer: This needs two separate pieces of logic because completeness and validity are different questions. Completeness: count rows where the column is NULL or an empty/whitespace-only string, and divide by the total row count to get a percentage. Validity: among the rows that ARE populated (excluding the ones already caught by the completeness check, since an empty value isn't a format failure, it's a missing value), count how many fail the specific format rule -- no '@' for Email, not exactly 10 digits for Phone. Keeping completeness and validity as separate counts, not combined into one pass/fail number, is what lets you actually tell which problem you have.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as two clearly separate aggregates in one query rather than trying to collapse everything into a single quality score, because the whole point of the exercise is being able to say 'X% missing' and 'Y% present-but-malformed' as two different findings. For completeness I use CASE WHEN ... IS NULL OR LTRIM(RTRIM(...)) = '' to catch both true NULLs and blank strings, since a column full of empty strings would otherwise sneak past a NULL-only check. For validity, I'm careful to scope it to non-null values only -- a NULL email isn't an invalid email, it's a missing one, and double-counting it in both buckets would overstate the problem. I use a simple LIKE pattern for the '@' check and a LIKE digit-mask pattern for the 10-digit phone check, since neither needs full regex for this level of rule.
questions.example:
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS TotalRows,

    -- Completeness
    SUM(CASE WHEN Email IS NULL OR LTRIM(RTRIM(Email)) = '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS MissingEmail,
    CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN Email IS NULL OR LTRIM(RTRIM(Email)) = '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS FLOAT) / COUNT(*) * 100 AS PctMissingEmail,
    SUM(CASE WHEN Phone IS NULL OR LTRIM(RTRIM(Phone)) = '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS MissingPhone,
    CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN Phone IS NULL OR LTRIM(RTRIM(Phone)) = '' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS FLOAT) / COUNT(*) * 100 AS PctMissingPhone,

    -- Validity (only among non-null values)
    SUM(CASE WHEN Email IS NOT NULL AND LTRIM(RTRIM(Email)) <> '' AND Email NOT LIKE '%_@_%.__%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS InvalidEmailFormat,
    SUM(CASE WHEN Phone IS NOT NULL AND LTRIM(RTRIM(Phone)) <> '' AND (LEN(Phone) <> 10 OR Phone LIKE '%[^0-9]%') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS InvalidPhoneFormat
FROM Customers;
commonMistakes: Catching only true NULLs and missing blank/whitespace-only strings in the completeness check
Double-counting NULL values as validity failures, inflating the invalid-format count
Using a validity pattern that's too strict or too loose for a basic sanity check (e.g., requiring a specific domain for email)
Reporting one combined pass/fail percentage instead of separate completeness and validity figures
keyPoints: Completeness and validity need separate logic and separate reported figures
A blank/whitespace string should be caught by the completeness check, same as a true NULL
Validity checks should be scoped to non-null, non-blank values only, to avoid double-counting
Simple LIKE/pattern checks are sufficient for a basic format rule like this

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes completeness counts/percentages for both columns
Correctly computes validity counts scoped to non-null values
Avoids double-counting NULLs as validity failures
Query is syntactically valid T-SQL
