questions.title: Writing a Business Glossary Entry for an Ambiguous Term
questions.prompt: Sales defines 'Active Customer' as anyone with an open account, while Finance defines it as anyone who purchased in the last 12 months. You're asked to resolve this for the enterprise glossary. Write the actual glossary entry (or entries) you'd propose, including the fields a real entry needs -- term, definition, synonyms, owner, related terms -- and explain how you'd handle the fact that two departments use the term differently.
questions.modelAnswer: The honest resolution here usually isn't forcing both departments onto one definition -- it's recognizing they're describing two genuinely different business concepts that happen to share a label, and giving each its own precisely named, precisely defined term. I'd propose: Term 1 -- 'Active Account' (Definition: a customer account that is currently open and not closed or suspended; Owner: Sales Operations; Synonyms: open account; Related Terms: Active Purchaser, Customer Status). Term 2 -- 'Active Purchaser' (Definition: a customer who has completed at least one purchase within the trailing 12 months; Owner: Finance; Synonyms: recent purchaser; Related Terms: Active Account, Customer Lifetime Value). The generic label 'Active Customer' should then be marked as deprecated/ambiguous in the glossary, pointing to both terms, so any report or request using the bare phrase 'Active Customer' gets flagged to specify which one is actually meant, rather than silently defaulting to whichever system happened to implement it first.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct isn't to referee which department is 'right,' because they're probably both right about their own use case -- they're just not talking about the same thing. I'd propose splitting the generic 'Active Customer' into two separately named, separately owned terms: 'Active Account' for Sales's account-status meaning, owned by Sales Operations, and 'Active Purchaser' for Finance's purchase-recency meaning, owned by Finance. Each gets a full entry -- a precise one-sentence definition, an owner who's accountable for keeping it accurate, any synonyms people already use for it, and a related-terms link pointing to the other one, specifically so anyone searching the glossary sees both and picks the one they actually mean. Then I'd mark the original ambiguous 'Active Customer' label itself as deprecated in the glossary with a note pointing to both replacements, so new reports stop using the vague version, and existing reports using it get flagged for review to figure out which one they actually meant all along.
commonMistakes: Trying to force both departments to agree on a single definition when they're describing genuinely different concepts
Writing a glossary entry without an owner, leaving nobody accountable for keeping the definition accurate
Not linking the two related terms to each other, leaving the ambiguity undiscoverable
Leaving the original ambiguous label active and undocumented instead of deprecating it with a pointer to the real terms
keyPoints: Two departments using the same label for different concepts usually calls for two distinct terms, not one compromise definition
A real glossary entry needs a precise definition, an accountable owner, synonyms, and related-term links
Related-term links are what make the disambiguation actually discoverable to someone searching the glossary
The original ambiguous label should be deprecated with a pointer, not left active alongside the new precise terms

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recognizes this as two distinct concepts rather than one to reconcile
Produces complete, well-formed glossary entries with all required fields
Links the two terms to each other as related terms
Addresses what happens to the original ambiguous label

questions.title: Producing an Impact Analysis Before a Breaking Change
questions.prompt: A DBA wants to drop the LegacyDiscountCode column from the Orders table, which has been unused by the application for over a year, 'to clean things up.' Walk through the concrete steps you'd take to produce an actual impact analysis before approving this, and what you'd look for at each step.
questions.modelAnswer: Step one: query whatever lineage/data map tooling is available for every known downstream consumer of Orders.LegacyDiscountCode -- views, stored procedures, ETL jobs, reports, BI semantic models -- rather than trusting 'unused by the application' as the full picture, since that phrase only describes one consumer, not every consumer. Step two, if lineage tooling is incomplete (common for an older column like this), search the actual code -- stored procedure definitions, SSIS/ADF package definitions, Power BI dataset queries, any ad hoc reporting scripts in source control -- for literal references to the column name. Step three: specifically look for consumers outside the obvious application layer -- scheduled exports, analysts pulling directly against the table with their own SQL, Excel workbooks with a live connection -- since these are exactly the kind of dependency that 'the application doesn't use it' misses entirely. Step four: compile the list of everything found, with an owner for each, and get explicit sign-off from every owner before approving the drop -- 'nobody flagged it' isn't the same as 'nothing depends on it.'
questions.professionalAnswer: The phrase that would stop me immediately is 'unused by the application,' because that's a claim about exactly one consumer, and there are almost always other consumers nobody thought to check. I'd start with whatever lineage or data map tool exists and pull every registered downstream dependency on that specific column -- views, procs, ETL jobs, BI models. Then, because a column that's been sitting unused for a year is exactly the kind of thing older lineage documentation might not have fully captured, I'd also do a literal text search across the actual code -- stored proc bodies, ETL package definitions, report dataset queries -- for the column name itself, since that catches things the lineage tool might have missed. The step I'd never skip: specifically asking around for anyone running ad hoc reports or Excel exports directly against this table with their own SQL, because that's the kind of dependency that lives entirely outside any tooling and is exactly what 'the application doesn't use it' was never going to tell me. Only once I have a real list with named owners attached would I get explicit sign-off from each of them -- not a general 'does anyone object' email, but direct confirmation from the people actually on that list.
commonMistakes: Accepting 'unused by the application' as sufficient evidence that nothing else depends on the column
Relying only on automated lineage tooling without a manual code search, when lineage documentation may be incomplete for an older object
Not specifically checking for ad hoc/direct-SQL consumers outside the application layer
Getting a general 'any objections?' sign-off instead of direct confirmation from each specific owner found
keyPoints: 'Unused by the application' only describes one consumer; it's not evidence about every consumer
Lineage/data map tooling should be the first check, but may be incomplete for an older or undocumented column
A manual code/query search catches dependencies lineage tooling might have missed
Ad hoc, direct-SQL, and export-based consumers are a common blind spot that needs an explicit check

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly starts with lineage/data map tooling rather than trusting the application claim alone
Includes a manual code/query search as a necessary supplement
Specifically checks for ad hoc/direct-access consumers outside the application
Requires explicit sign-off from named owners before approving the change

questions.title: Identifying Deduplication Candidates and Applying a Survivorship Rule
questions.prompt: Write SQL against a Customers table (CustomerID, FirstName, LastName, Phone, Email) that identifies candidate duplicate records by matching on normalized LastName + Phone (ignoring case and non-digit characters in Phone). Then describe the survivorship rule you'd apply to decide which of the matched records' Email value becomes the golden record's Email.
questions.modelAnswer: Normalize both matching attributes before comparing: UPPER(LastName) to remove case sensitivity, and strip non-digit characters from Phone (a chain of REPLACE calls, or a cleaner regex-based approach if the platform supports it) so '(555) 123-4567' and '5551234567' are recognized as the same number. Group by the two normalized values and use HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to surface groups with more than one record -- those are candidate duplicates, deliberately labeled 'candidate' because this is deterministic exact-match logic on two attributes, not a true fuzzy/probabilistic match, and it should be reviewed by a data steward before anything is auto-merged. For the Email survivorship rule: since the question doesn't give a reliable 'most recently verified' signal, a reasonable default is a tiered rule -- prefer a non-null Email over a null one, and if both candidate records have a non-null Email, flag the group for manual steward review rather than guessing, since silently picking one real email over another real email risks losing a legitimately different, still-valid contact point.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd normalize before I ever compare: last name uppercased so case differences don't create false non-matches, and phone stripped down to just digits so formatting differences don't hide an actual match. Grouping on those two normalized values and filtering to groups with more than one row gives me my candidate list -- and I'd be careful to call it exactly that, candidates, not confirmed duplicates, because matching on just two attributes is a blunt, deterministic rule that will have false positives (two different people who happen to share a last name and, less likely, an old shared landline) and shouldn't auto-merge anything on its own. For the Email survivorship piece, I'd resist the urge to just pick one arbitrarily -- if one record has an email and the other doesn't, the non-null one obviously wins. But if both records have a real, different email address, that's not a case I'd resolve automatically at all, because I have no signal here telling me which one is actually still valid -- that's exactly the kind of decision I'd route to a steward for manual review rather than silently discarding someone's real contact information.
questions.example:
-- Candidate duplicates: normalized LastName + Phone
SELECT
    UPPER(LastName) AS NormalizedLastName,
    REPLACE(REPLACE(REPLACE(REPLACE(Phone, '(', ''), ')', ''), '-', ''), ' ', '') AS NormalizedPhone,
    COUNT(*) AS MatchCount,
    STRING_AGG(CAST(CustomerID AS VARCHAR), ', ') AS CandidateCustomerIDs
FROM Customers
GROUP BY
    UPPER(LastName),
    REPLACE(REPLACE(REPLACE(REPLACE(Phone, '(', ''), ')', ''), '-', ''), ' ', '')
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
commonMistakes: Comparing LastName and Phone without normalizing case or stripping formatting characters, missing real matches
Treating the output of a two-attribute match as confirmed duplicates rather than candidates needing steward review
Auto-merging or auto-discarding an email value when both candidate records have different, non-null emails
Not having any survivorship logic at all for the null-vs-non-null case, which is the one case that's actually safe to resolve automatically
keyPoints: Normalization (case folding, stripping formatting) is required before comparing matching attributes
A two-attribute exact match produces candidates, not confirmed duplicates, and needs steward review before merging
Non-null should survive over null by default for a survivorship rule
Two conflicting non-null values should route to manual review rather than being resolved automatically

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly normalizes both LastName and Phone before matching
Correctly groups and filters to surface only groups with more than one record
Proposes a sound, specific survivorship rule for the Email field
Notes this is candidate matching requiring review, not an automatic merge

questions.title: Masking a Sensitive Column for Non-Privileged Roles
questions.prompt: Write T-SQL that applies Dynamic Data Masking to an SSN column on an Employees table so that users without the UNMASK permission see only the last four digits, and show the GRANT statement that would let a specific HR role see the real value.
questions.modelAnswer: Dynamic Data Masking is applied as a column property with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... ADD MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = ...). For partially exposing only the last four digits of an SSN, the partial() masking function lets you specify how many characters to expose at the start, a padding string for the masked middle portion, and how many characters to expose at the end. Any user without UNMASK permission querying that column sees the masked version automatically, with no change needed to their queries. To let a specific role see the real value, GRANT UNMASK to that role specifically, rather than to all users or to a broad built-in role -- UNMASK should be a deliberately narrow grant, not a default.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd apply the mask directly on the column definition rather than trying to mask it in every query that touches it, since Dynamic Data Masking is designed to apply automatically and consistently everywhere the column is read, which is the whole point -- one place to maintain, not one per query. For an SSN specifically, partial() is the right function because I want to control exactly which characters show -- zero visible at the start, a fixed mask like 'XXX-XX-' in the middle, and the last four digits exposed at the end, which matches how SSNs are commonly partially displayed in the first place. The GRANT is the other half of this and just as important -- I'd grant UNMASK only to the specific HR role that genuinely needs the real value, never broadly, because every UNMASK grant is a standing exception to the protection the masking rule was supposed to provide, and it should be reviewed periodically just like any other privileged access grant.
commonMistakes: Trying to implement masking logic in application code or views instead of on the column itself, creating inconsistent exposure
Granting UNMASK broadly (e.g., to all authenticated users or a wide built-in role) instead of a narrow, specific role
Forgetting that members of db_owner or sysadmin bypass masking entirely regardless of UNMASK grants
Getting the partial() function's argument order wrong, exposing the wrong portion of the value
keyPoints: Dynamic Data Masking is applied as a column property via ALTER TABLE ... ADD MASKED WITH
partial() lets you control exactly which characters are exposed versus masked
UNMASK permission should be granted narrowly to a specific role, not broadly
Masking is bypassed by elevated roles like db_owner/sysadmin regardless of UNMASK grants

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly applies masking using the partial() function with the right arguments
Correctly grants UNMASK to a specific, narrow role
Explains the automatic, consistent-everywhere nature of the masking
Code is syntactically valid T-SQL

questions.title: Configuring a Scan in Microsoft Purview
questions.prompt: Walk through, step by step, what you'd actually configure to scan a new Azure SQL Database source in Microsoft Purview for the first time -- from registering the source to the scan actually running on a schedule. Name the concrete settings involved at each step, not just the high-level phases.
questions.modelAnswer: First, register the data source: in the Purview Data Map, add a new source, choose the Azure SQL Database source type, and provide the server and database connection details. Second, set up a credential Purview will scan with -- typically a managed identity or a service principal with read access to the database, or SQL authentication stored securely in an integration with Azure Key Vault, and if the database isn't reachable directly (private network), a self-hosted integration runtime. Third, create the actual scan against the registered source: choose the scope (specific schemas/tables, or the entire database), and select a scan rule set -- either the default system rule set or a custom one specifying which classification rules (like SSN, credit card, email patterns) should run during scanning. Fourth, choose a trigger: run once, or set a recurring schedule (daily, weekly) for ongoing scanning as the source changes. Finally, after the scan runs, check the scan history for success/failure status and review how many assets were discovered and classified.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this in the actual order I'd click through it, because each step genuinely depends on the one before it. Registration first -- add the Azure SQL Database as a source, give it a name, point it at the right server and database. Then credentials -- this is the step people sometimes underestimate, because Purview needs a real way to connect and read that database, whether that's a managed identity with the right database role granted, or a service principal/SQL login whose secret lives in Key Vault rather than typed in directly, plus a self-hosted integration runtime if the database sits behind a private network Purview's cloud scanning can't reach directly. Once the source can actually be read, I create the scan itself: pick the scope so I'm not scanning more than I need to, and pick a scan rule set -- I'd actually open up what's in the default system rule set first rather than assuming it covers everything, since a custom classification might be needed depending on what kind of sensitive data this source holds. Then the trigger -- for a source I expect to keep changing, I'd set it recurring rather than one-and-done, since a single scan only reflects the schema and data at that moment. Last step, and one I wouldn't skip, is actually checking the scan run's history afterward -- confirming it succeeded and looking at how many assets and classifications it actually found, rather than assuming a scan that was configured correctly also ran correctly.
commonMistakes: Skipping or underspecifying the credential/authentication step, assuming Purview can just connect without explicit access configured
Not checking whether a self-hosted integration runtime is needed for a source behind a private network
Assuming the default scan rule set covers every classification needed without reviewing it
Running a one-time scan for a source that will keep changing, instead of setting a recurring schedule
keyPoints: Registration, credentials, scan configuration, and scheduling are four distinct, sequential steps
Credentials often require a managed identity or service principal, plus a self-hosted integration runtime for private networks
The scan rule set determines which classification rules actually run during scanning
A recurring schedule is appropriate for sources that change over time; checking scan history confirms it actually worked

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes source registration with concrete settings
Correctly describes credential/connectivity configuration
Correctly describes scan scope and scan rule set configuration
Correctly describes scheduling and verifying scan history

questions.title: Diagnosing a deadlock between two ETL jobs
questions.prompt: Two nightly stored procedures occasionally fail with a deadlock error when they run at overlapping times, each updating the same two tables. Explain what a deadlock is, how SQL Server resolves it automatically, and two concrete things you'd change to prevent it from recurring.
questions.modelAnswer: Blocking happens whenever one transaction needs a lock another transaction already holds, and simply waits -- this is normal and expected. A deadlock is the special case where Transaction A is waiting on a lock held by Transaction B, while B is simultaneously waiting on a lock held by A -- neither can ever proceed. SQL Server detects this automatically and picks one transaction as the 'deadlock victim,' rolling it back and raising an error, while the other transaction proceeds normally. To prevent recurrence: (1) access the two tables in the same order in both procedures -- a common deadlock cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; and (2) keep transactions as short as possible, doing only what genuinely needs to be atomic inside BEGIN/COMMIT, so locks are held for the shortest possible window and the overlap that triggers the deadlock has a smaller chance of occurring.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by reassuring whoever's asking that blocking itself isn't a bug -- it's how isolation is enforced any time two transactions genuinely need the same data at the same moment. A deadlock is the specific, more serious case: A is waiting on a lock B holds, B is waiting on a lock A holds, and neither can ever win -- it's a true standoff. SQL Server doesn't just hang forever; it detects the cycle and picks a 'deadlock victim' to roll back automatically, which is why the application sees an error and needs to retry. For the actual fix, the first thing I'd check is whether both procedures touch the two tables in a different order -- that's the single most common cause, and standardizing the access order so both procedures always touch, say, Table A before Table B usually eliminates it outright. Second, I'd look at whether either transaction is doing more than it needs to inside BEGIN/COMMIT -- unrelated reads, validation logic -- and trim the transaction down to just the atomic part, since shorter transactions hold locks for less time and collide less often.
commonMistakes: Treating a deadlock the same as ordinary blocking -- blocking is normal, a deadlock is a genuine, unresolvable standoff
Assuming SQL Server will just hang forever instead of recognizing it auto-detects and resolves deadlocks
Fixing the symptom by adding a retry loop in the application without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Making a transaction longer by adding error handling or logging inside it, which increases lock duration
keyPoints: Blocking is normal; a deadlock is two transactions waiting on each other with no way out
SQL Server auto-detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen 'victim' transaction
The victim's application should retry the transaction
Accessing tables in a consistent order across procedures prevents most deadlocks
Shortening transactions reduces how long locks are held and how often collisions occur

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes blocking from a deadlock
Correctly explains SQL Server's automatic deadlock resolution
Proposes consistent table access order as a concrete fix
Proposes shortening transactions as a concrete fix

questions.title: A query got slow after it used to be fast
questions.prompt: A report query that filters WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013 used to run instantly and now takes minutes as the table has grown. There is an index on OrderDate. Diagnose why the index isn't helping, and rewrite the WHERE clause so it is.
questions.modelAnswer: The predicate is non-SARGable: wrapping the OrderDate column in the YEAR() function forces SQL Server to compute YEAR(OrderDate) for every single row before it can compare against 2013, which means the index on the raw OrderDate column can't be used -- it stores actual dates, not year-extracted values. This was barely noticeable on a small table (a full scan of a few hundred rows is instant either way), but as the table grows into the millions of rows, the same non-SARGable predicate turns a sub-second query into one that takes minutes. The fix is to rewrite the condition so the column itself is left untouched, and transform the comparison value instead: WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01'. This asks the identical logical question but lets SQL Server use the index on OrderDate to jump directly to the matching range.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a textbook SARGability problem, and the giveaway is right there in the WHERE clause -- there's a function wrapped around the column. Any time I see YEAR(SomeDateColumn), UPPER(SomeColumn), or similar, my first instinct is: the index on that raw column can't be used, because SQL Server would have to transform every row's value before it could compare it, and an index doesn't store transformed values. The reason it 'used to be fast' is simply table size -- a full scan is invisible on a small table and brutal on a large one, so this kind of bug often doesn't show up until data volume grows past some threshold. The fix is always the same shape: stop transforming the column, and transform the comparison value instead. Instead of asking 'what year is this date in,' I ask 'is this date within the 2013 calendar year range' -- same answer, but now the raw OrderDate column is untouched in the comparison, so the existing index can be used for a range scan instead of a full scan.
commonMistakes: Blaming the index itself ('the index must be corrupt/fragmented') instead of the predicate wrapping the column
Rewriting to BETWEEN '2013-01-01' AND '2013-12-31' and accidentally excluding rows with a time component on Dec 31
Not recognizing other common non-SARGable patterns like UPPER(column) = 'X' or a leading-wildcard LIKE '%text'
Assuming the problem only appears with YEAR() and missing that any function on the column causes the same issue
keyPoints: SARGable means the predicate can use an index directly; non-SARGable forces a full scan
Wrapping the column in a function (YEAR, UPPER, etc.) makes a predicate non-SARGable
Fix by transforming the comparison value instead of the column
The performance gap only becomes visible as table size grows

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the predicate as non-SARGable and explains why
Correctly explains why this matters more as the table grows
Provides a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite
Rewrite correctly handles the full year's date range without off-by-one errors

questions.title: A report is hanging, but there's no deadlock error
questions.prompt: Users report that a dashboard query has been 'just spinning' for several minutes, but no deadlock error ever appears. Explain the difference between this situation and a deadlock, how you'd identify the actual head blocker, and what you'd check before deciding to kill the blocking session.
questions.modelAnswer: This is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- a deadlock is a genuine standoff that SQL Server detects and resolves automatically within seconds by killing a victim; it never just hangs indefinitely. Plain blocking, by contrast, can hang as long as whatever is holding the lock keeps holding it, because there's no cycle for SQL Server to detect -- one session is simply waiting its turn behind another, and nothing resolves that automatically. To find the actual head blocker, I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests, specifically looking at the blocking_session_id column -- the session with a non-zero blocking_session_id is being blocked, and the session that ID points to (which itself usually shows blocking_session_id = 0) is the head blocker actually holding the lock everyone's waiting on. Before killing that session, I'd check what it's actually doing -- its SQL text, and whether it's an open, uncommitted transaction (an application that opened a transaction and is sitting idle, or a long-running batch job that's legitimately mid-write). Killing a session mid-write rolls back whatever it was doing, which can be worse than the wait itself if it's a large, mostly-finished operation -- so I'd rather understand what it's doing and consider letting it finish or committing/rolling it back cleanly than reflexively kill it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd clarify, because it changes the whole response, is that this isn't a deadlock -- SQL Server resolves deadlocks on its own, usually within seconds, by picking a victim and rolling it back. If nothing has errored and the query is just sitting there, that's plain blocking: one session waiting on a lock another session is holding, with no cycle, so nothing forces a resolution automatically. My first query is always against sys.dm_exec_requests, looking at blocking_session_id -- that tells me directly who's blocked and, by following the chain, who the actual head blocker is, as opposed to the session that looks blocked but is itself only blocked by someone else further up. Once I've got the head blocker's session ID, I'd pull its actual SQL text and check whether it's sitting inside an open transaction that was never committed, versus genuinely mid-execution on a big write. That distinction decides what I do next -- if it's an application bug that opened a transaction and forgot to close it, killing the session is reasonable and I'd also flag that bug separately. If it's a legitimate long-running batch load that's 90% done, killing it rolls back all of that work and probably makes things worse, so I'd rather let it finish, or coordinate with whoever owns that job before touching it.
questions.example:
-- Find who's blocking whom
SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, status
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests
WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0;

-- Follow the chain to the head blocker (blocking_session_id = 0, but others point to it)
-- Then inspect what the head blocker is actually running:
SELECT text
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) t
WHERE r.session_id = @HeadBlockerSessionId;
commonMistakes: Treating any hanging query as a deadlock, when a true deadlock is auto-resolved within seconds, not left hanging
Killing the first blocked session found instead of tracing blocking_session_id to the actual head blocker
Killing a session without checking whether it's mid-write on a legitimate long-running job
Not distinguishing an application bug (an abandoned open transaction) from a genuinely busy, legitimate session
keyPoints: A hanging query with no error is ordinary blocking, not a deadlock -- deadlocks auto-resolve quickly
sys.dm_exec_requests' blocking_session_id column traces the blocking chain to the actual head blocker
Check what the head blocker is actually doing before killing it -- an abandoned transaction vs. a legitimate long write
Killing a session mid-write rolls back its work, which can be worse than waiting for it to finish

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes ordinary blocking from a deadlock
Correctly identifies how to find the head blocker (sys.dm_exec_requests / blocking_session_id)
Explains what to check before killing the blocking session
Provides correct, relevant diagnostic SQL

questions.title: A Covering Index Isn't Helping, and Nobody Knows Why
questions.prompt: A table has a nonclustered index covering exactly the columns a report query needs, but the query's execution plan still shows a full scan instead of using the index. The query is SELECT * FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. What's the most likely cause, and how would you fix the query?
questions.modelAnswer: SELECT * is almost certainly the cause. A covering index only helps when the query asks for columns the index actually includes; SELECT * asks for every column in the table, regardless of what's actually needed, which defeats the index's coverage the moment even one requested column isn't part of it. SQL Server then has to fall back to either a Key Lookup for each matching row or a full scan, depending on cost, instead of satisfying the query entirely from the narrower index. The fix is to name only the columns the report genuinely needs instead of SELECT *: SELECT SalesOrderID, ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail WHERE ProductID = 712. If those four columns are exactly what the covering index includes, the optimizer can now satisfy the entire query from the index alone, without ever touching the underlying table.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before touching the index, I'd actually look at the execution plan and the exact columns requested, because 'should use the index but doesn't' almost always traces back to the SELECT list, not the index definition. SELECT * is the first thing I'd check, because it's such a common habit and such a direct cause: if the index only covers four specific columns and the query asks for all fifteen columns on the table via *, the index simply can't satisfy that request on its own, and SQL Server has to go fetch the rest from the table itself — either via a Key Lookup per row or by abandoning the index entirely for a full scan, depending on how many rows are involved. The fix is almost always just naming the specific columns the report actually displays instead of *. I'd also double check that the index's included columns genuinely match what the report needs, because if even one required column is missing from the index, the same fallback happens no matter how narrowly I write the SELECT list.
commonMistakes: Assuming the index itself must be broken or missing, without checking what columns the query actually requests
Rebuilding or recreating the index before checking the SELECT list, missing the actual cause
Not verifying the index's included columns genuinely cover everything the trimmed SELECT list needs
Fixing this one query but not checking other queries against the same table for the identical SELECT * habit
keyPoints: SELECT * requests every column, defeating a covering index that only includes some of them
The fallback is a Key Lookup per row, or a full scan, instead of satisfying the query from the index alone
The fix is naming exactly the columns actually needed
The index's included columns must still genuinely match what's requested for this fix to work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies SELECT * as the likely cause
Correctly explains why it defeats a covering index
Provides a correct fix naming specific columns
Notes the fix depends on the index already covering those exact columns

questions.title: The Completeness Dashboard Says 100%, But the Report is Full of Garbage
questions.prompt: A data quality dashboard reports 100% completeness on the Customer.Email column -- zero NULLs. A marketing team member says half their email campaign bounced because the addresses are garbage ('test@test', 'none', single characters). Diagnose the gap, and describe the specific check you'd add.
questions.modelAnswer: The dashboard is measuring exactly what it was built to measure -- the presence of a value -- and it's correctly reporting that nothing is NULL. The gap is that completeness was never going to catch this problem, because none of the bounced addresses are missing; they're present, just wrong. 'test@test', 'none', and single-character strings all pass a NOT NULL check with room to spare. The fix is adding a validity check that was never there: a pattern rule testing whether the value actually looks like a real email address (contains '@' followed by a domain with a dot), plus a specific denylist check for known placeholder values that technically match a loose pattern but are obviously not real addresses ('test@test', 'none', 'n/a'). Both checks should report separately from completeness, and ideally the dashboard itself should show completeness and validity as two distinct figures so this gap doesn't recur silently next time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't call this a bug in the dashboard -- it's doing exactly what a completeness check does, which is check for presence, not correctness. The actual problem is that completeness was the only check running, and completeness was never capable of catching this category of issue in the first place; every one of those bounced addresses is a non-null string, so it sailed right through. What I'd add is a genuine validity check: a basic shape test for whether something resembles a real email address, and separately, a denylist for known junk values that technically contain an '@' or technically aren't blank but are obviously placeholders -- 'none,' 'n/a,' single characters. I'd also flag the dashboard design itself as part of the real fix here, not just the missing check -- if completeness is the only number shown, people will keep assuming 'complete' means 'correct,' and this exact conversation will happen again on a different column.
questions.example:
-- What was already running (completeness only) -- correctly reports 0 missing
SELECT COUNT(*) AS Total, SUM(CASE WHEN Email IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS Missing FROM Customer;

-- What was missing: a validity + known-junk check
SELECT
    SUM(CASE WHEN Email NOT LIKE '%_@_%.__%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS BadFormat,
    SUM(CASE WHEN LOWER(LTRIM(RTRIM(Email))) IN ('test@test', 'none', 'n/a') OR LEN(LTRIM(RTRIM(Email))) <= 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS KnownJunkOrTooShort
FROM Customer;
commonMistakes: Assuming the dashboard's completeness check must be broken instead of recognizing it's just measuring the wrong dimension
Adding a validity check that only tests for the presence of '@', missing obvious junk values like 'none' that already contain no '@' but would pass a looser check
Not addressing the dashboard design itself, which presents completeness as if it were a full quality signal
Treating this as a one-off fix for Email instead of checking whether other columns have the same completeness-only blind spot
keyPoints: A completeness check cannot catch garbage data -- it only checks for presence, not correctness
The fix requires adding a genuinely separate validity check, including a denylist for known placeholder values
Validity and completeness should be reported as distinct figures, not collapsed into one score
This same gap likely exists on other columns and is worth auditing proactively

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses that completeness cannot catch this class of problem
Proposes a concrete validity check including a junk-value denylist
Provides correct, relevant SQL for the new check
Addresses the dashboard presentation gap as part of the fix

questions.title: A Reconciliation Check Passes, But the Totals in Two Systems Still Don't Match
questions.prompt: An automated cross-system reconciliation check compares daily order counts between the OLTP system and the data warehouse and reports a match every night. Finance says the two systems' revenue totals have been off by a growing amount for weeks. Diagnose what the reconciliation check is actually missing, and what additional check should be added.
questions.modelAnswer: The existing check validates row-count parity -- it confirms the same number of orders landed in both systems -- which is a legitimate but narrow check: it says nothing about whether each individual order's monetary amount matches between systems. A count match is fully consistent with a value mismatch -- the right number of orders could have arrived in the warehouse with a rounding error, a currency conversion bug, or a partial/duplicate line-item load on some subset of them, and the count would never notice, since it's not looking at amounts at all. The fix is adding a value-level reconciliation: comparing SUM(OrderTotal) between source and warehouse for the same date range or order set, not just COUNT(*). If the sums diverge, drilling down to find which specific orders' amounts don't match between the two systems is the next step to isolate the actual defect, since a count-only check gives no hint about which orders are responsible.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a classic case of a check that's correct but answering a narrower question than the one that actually matters. Matching order counts tells you the right number of rows made it across -- it genuinely rules out whole orders going missing or duplicating -- but it has zero visibility into whether each order's dollar amount is right once it lands. A growing dollar discrepancy with a stable count match points pretty specifically at something wrong with the amounts themselves -- a currency conversion step that's drifting, a rounding rule applied inconsistently, or maybe a line-item join in the ETL that's double-counting on some subset of orders while the header-level count stays correct. The check I'd add is a straightforward SUM(OrderTotal) comparison between source and warehouse over the same window, run alongside the existing count check rather than replacing it. And once that shows a gap, I wouldn't stop there -- I'd want to narrow it down to the actual order IDs where source and warehouse amounts disagree, because that's what actually tells you where in the pipeline the bug lives.
commonMistakes: Assuming a passing count-based reconciliation means the data is fully consistent between systems
Not distinguishing a row-count check from a value/amount-level check as two genuinely different validations
Adding a value check but running it in isolation instead of alongside the existing count check
Stopping at 'the sums don't match' without drilling into which specific orders are responsible
keyPoints: A count-based reconciliation only validates that the right number of rows arrived, not that their values are correct
A growing value discrepancy with a stable count match points to an amount-level defect, not a missing/duplicate row
The fix is adding a SUM(OrderTotal)-level reconciliation alongside the existing count check
Isolating which specific orders diverge is necessary to actually find and fix the root defect

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that the existing check only validates row counts, not values
Correctly proposes a value-level (SUM) reconciliation as the missing check
Suggests plausible root causes consistent with count-match/value-mismatch
Describes drilling down to specific orders to isolate the defect

questions.title: Two Dashboards Report Different 'Revenue' Numbers, and Both Teams Say Theirs is Right
questions.prompt: The Sales dashboard and the Finance dashboard both display a metric called 'Revenue,' and they consistently disagree by about 8%. Both teams insist their number is correct. Diagnose the likely root cause from a metadata/glossary perspective, and describe how you'd resolve it.
questions.modelAnswer: This is very unlikely to be a data bug in either dashboard -- it's much more likely a missing or inconsistent glossary definition. 'Revenue' is a term that commonly means genuinely different things depending on department: Sales often counts booked or contracted revenue the moment a deal closes, while Finance typically counts recognized revenue, net of returns, refunds, or deferred recognition rules. Without a single governed glossary term defining exactly what 'Revenue' means at the enterprise level, each team built a calculation that's internally correct for the question they're actually answering, and the two numbers were never going to match because they're not measuring the same thing. The resolution isn't to 'fix' either dashboard's calculation -- it's to bring both teams together, get an explicit governed definition (most realistically, two separately named terms like 'Booked Revenue' and 'Recognized Revenue'), and relabel each dashboard with the specific governed term it actually reports, instead of the ambiguous generic label both have been using.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before touching either dashboard's query, I'd bet this isn't a calculation bug at all -- it's a definitions problem. A consistent 8% gap, not a random or growing one, is the signature of two systematically different but each internally consistent calculations, which is exactly what you'd expect if Sales is counting revenue the moment a deal is booked and Finance is counting it only once it's actually recognized under accounting rules, net of whatever adjustments apply. Neither team is lying about their number being correct -- they're both right, for different definitions of the same word. The fix isn't picking a winner; it's getting both teams in a room, through whatever glossary governance process exists, and landing on explicit, separately named terms -- 'Booked Revenue' and 'Recognized Revenue' is the obvious split -- each with its own precise definition and owner. Then both dashboards get relabeled to show the specific governed term they actually calculate, so the next person who sees two different 'Revenue' numbers at least knows they're looking at two clearly different, correctly labeled things instead of an unexplained discrepancy.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a data quality or calculation bug and trying to debug the SQL before checking the definitions
Assuming one team's number must be wrong instead of considering both could be correct for different definitions
Picking a single winning definition unilaterally instead of resolving it through glossary governance with both teams
Fixing the underlying confusion without relabeling the dashboards, leaving the ambiguous generic label in place
keyPoints: A consistent, non-random discrepancy between two 'correct' calculations points to a definitions gap, not a bug
Different departments commonly use the same business term (e.g. Revenue) to mean genuinely different things
Resolution requires glossary governance: explicit, separately named and defined terms, not picking a winner
Both dashboards should be relabeled with the specific governed term they actually report

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses this as a glossary/definitions gap, not a data bug
Gives a plausible, specific explanation of how Sales and Finance revenue definitions differ
Proposes resolving through governance with explicit, separately named terms
Proposes relabeling both dashboards rather than silently picking one number

questions.title: A Report Broke After an Upstream Rename, and Lineage Said Nothing Depended on It
questions.prompt: An upstream team renamed a column in a source table. The lineage documentation for that table said no downstream reports depended on it, but a finance report broke that morning anyway. Diagnose what's likely wrong with the lineage documentation, and what you'd change going forward.
questions.modelAnswer: The lineage documentation is very likely manually maintained and stale. Manual lineage docs only reflect whatever dependencies someone remembered to record at some point in the past -- they don't automatically detect a new report that was built directly against the source table afterward, and they silently drift out of date every time that happens without anyone going back to update the document. The actual dependency clearly existed; the documentation simply never captured it, probably because the finance report was built after the lineage doc was last updated, or was built by someone who queried the source table directly without going through whatever process would have triggered a documentation update. Going forward, the real fix is moving toward automated lineage capture -- a tool that parses actual SQL, ETL, or report queries to discover real dependencies as they're created -- rather than relying on a manually maintained document that's only ever as current as the last person who remembered to update it. As an interim safeguard, any planned upstream change should also include an actual impact query run against the real environment, not just a check against the documentation.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first assumption here is that the lineage documentation is manual, or at least manually supplemented, because this is exactly the failure mode manual lineage has -- it's a snapshot of what someone knew and wrote down at some point, not a living reflection of what's actually querying the source table today. Somewhere between whenever that document was last updated and this morning, the finance report either got built directly against the source table, or an existing report started referencing this column, and nobody went back and updated the lineage doc to reflect it -- which is an entirely normal, unsurprising way for manual documentation to drift, not a one-off mistake by a careless person. The actual fix isn't 'be more careful updating the doc next time' -- it's reducing how much this relies on someone remembering to do that at all, by moving toward automated lineage tooling that discovers dependencies by actually parsing the queries hitting that table, so a new consumer gets captured the moment it starts running rather than whenever someone happens to document it. Until that's in place, I'd also insist that any upstream change goes through an actual impact query against the live environment before the change ships, instead of trusting the document as the final word.
commonMistakes: Assuming the renamed-column team did something wrong instead of identifying the stale documentation as the root cause
Trusting lineage documentation as current without checking how and when it's actually maintained
Fixing this single gap in the document without addressing the underlying manual-maintenance process that let it go stale
Not proposing automated lineage capture or a live impact-verification step as the actual long-term fix
keyPoints: Manually maintained lineage documentation only reflects what was captured at some point in the past, and drifts stale over time
A new or undocumented consumer built directly against a source table explains the gap between the doc and reality
Automated lineage capture (parsing real queries) is the structural fix, not more diligent manual updates
An interim safeguard is running a live impact query before any upstream change, rather than trusting documentation alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses stale/manual lineage documentation as the likely root cause
Explains concretely how such documentation drifts out of date
Proposes automated lineage capture as the structural long-term fix
Proposes a concrete interim safeguard (live impact verification before changes)

questions.title: The MDM System Auto-Merged Two Different People Into One Golden Record
questions.prompt: Your MDM matching process auto-merged two customer records into a single golden record. It turns out they're two different people who happen to share a name and live in the same apartment complex. Diagnose what likely went wrong with the matching configuration, and describe the remediation process, not just the technical fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The likely cause is that the match threshold for auto-merging was set too loosely for this match type, or the matching rule relied on too few, or too weak, distinguishing attributes -- probably name plus address similarity alone, with no stronger differentiator like phone, email, or date of birth in the mix. Two genuinely different people who share a name and live in the same building would score highly on exactly those two attributes, pushing the match score above the auto-merge threshold even though they're not actually the same entity. The remediation is not just a technical fix to the threshold -- it requires a formal un-merge/stewardship process: a data steward needs to review the specific merged record, split it back into its two original source records (not simply delete the golden record, since downstream systems may have already consumed the incorrect merged version and need to be corrected too). Beyond fixing this one record, any auto-merge rule operating at this risk level -- matching on weak, easily-coincidental attributes -- should likely be downgraded to a manual-review queue instead of fully automatic merging going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first guess is that whatever attributes the matching rule relied on just weren't distinguishing enough for this specific case -- probably name and address, and nothing stronger like date of birth or a verified phone/email, which means two unrelated people who happen to share a last name and an apartment complex looked, numerically, close enough to merge automatically. That's a configuration problem, not a one-off fluke -- if it happened once for this reason, it's happened silently for other coincidental matches too, just without anyone noticing yet. But I wouldn't treat the fix as just 'tighten the threshold and move on' -- there's a real remediation process here: a steward needs to actually look at this specific merged record, confirm it really is two different people, and split it back into its two original source records, which is more involved than deleting the bad golden record, because anything downstream that already consumed the wrong merged version -- a report, a marketing list, a billing system -- may need its own correction too. And separately from fixing this one case, I'd flag the broader matching rule itself for review -- if it's auto-merging on attributes this coincidental, it probably shouldn't be fully automatic at all; routing borderline matches to a steward for manual confirmation is the safer long-term setup.
commonMistakes: Treating this as purely a technical bug and only adjusting the match threshold without a formal remediation process
Deleting the bad golden record instead of splitting it back into its two original source records
Not checking whether downstream systems already consumed the incorrect merged golden record
Not reviewing whether the broader matching rule should be downgraded to manual review given this risk
keyPoints: A loose threshold or too few/weak matching attributes likely allowed a coincidental match to auto-merge
Remediation requires a formal steward-led un-merge/split process, not just deleting the bad record
Downstream systems that already consumed the bad golden record may need their own correction
The matching rule itself, not just this one case, should be reviewed for whether auto-merge is appropriate at this risk level

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses a loose threshold or weak matching attributes as the likely cause
Describes a proper steward-led remediation process, not just a technical fix
Addresses downstream systems that may have consumed the bad merge
Proposes reviewing the broader matching rule's risk level going forward

questions.title: A 'Read-Only' Analyst Can See Unmasked SSNs
questions.prompt: An analyst whose role is supposed to be read-only reporting access is able to see full, unmasked SSNs in a report, even though dynamic data masking is configured on that column. Diagnose the likely cause, and what you'd check first.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely causes, in rough order of likelihood: the analyst's role, or a group they belong to, was granted the UNMASK permission directly or indirectly -- possibly inherited from a broader role grant originally made for a different purpose and never scoped down; the report queries the data through a view or stored procedure that reconstructs or re-exposes the value in a way that bypasses the masking rule, or masking was applied inconsistently across the different objects that expose that column; or the analyst's account has elevated membership, such as db_owner or sysadmin, which bypasses Dynamic Data Masking entirely regardless of any UNMASK grants. The first thing to check is querying sys.database_permissions and role memberships to see whether UNMASK reaches this login through any path, direct or inherited, and separately checking whether the report's actual query path -- the specific view or stored procedure it uses -- touches the masked column directly or through an object that was never masked in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start from the assumption that 'read-only' as a role name doesn't actually guarantee anything about UNMASK -- those are two completely separate permission concepts, and it's entirely possible for a role to be read-only in terms of not being able to write data while still, through some grant somewhere, having UNMASK. My first query would be against sys.database_permissions and the role membership chain, tracing whether UNMASK reaches this specific login through any path -- directly, through a group, through a role they were added to for an unrelated reason. In parallel, I'd check the actual report's query path, because masking has to be applied on every object that exposes the column -- if the report goes through a view that was created before masking was added to the base table, or a stored procedure that does something unusual with the column, it's possible masking just never got applied consistently across every object touching that data. And I wouldn't rule out the blunt possibility either -- checking whether this analyst's account somehow has db_owner or sysadmin, since that bypasses masking completely and would explain the symptom immediately regardless of any UNMASK investigation.
questions.example:
-- Check who actually has UNMASK, directly or via role membership
SELECT dp.state_desc, dp.permission_name, pr.name AS GranteeName
FROM sys.database_permissions dp
JOIN sys.database_principals pr ON dp.grantee_principal_id = pr.principal_id
WHERE dp.permission_name = 'UNMASK';

-- Check for elevated membership that bypasses masking entirely
SELECT roles.name AS RoleName, members.name AS MemberName
FROM sys.database_role_members rm
JOIN sys.database_principals roles ON rm.role_principal_id = roles.principal_id
JOIN sys.database_principals members ON rm.member_principal_id = members.principal_id
WHERE roles.name IN ('db_owner');
commonMistakes: Assuming a role named 'read-only' automatically means it can't have UNMASK, when the two are unrelated permissions
Checking only direct grants and missing UNMASK inherited through group or role membership
Not checking whether the report's actual query path (a view or proc) bypasses the masked column entirely
Overlooking elevated membership like db_owner/sysadmin, which bypasses masking regardless of UNMASK
keyPoints: A role name like 'read-only' says nothing about whether UNMASK was granted -- they're separate permissions
UNMASK can reach a user indirectly through group or role membership, not just a direct grant
Masking must be applied consistently across every object (table, view, proc) that exposes the column
Elevated membership (db_owner/sysadmin) bypasses Dynamic Data Masking entirely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies UNMASK grant (direct or inherited) as a likely cause
Correctly identifies inconsistent masking across views/procs as a likely cause
Correctly identifies elevated membership bypassing masking as a possibility
Provides correct, relevant diagnostic SQL

questions.title: A Purview Scan Finishes Clean, But Obvious SSN Columns Aren't Classified
questions.prompt: A Purview scan against a SQL Server source completes successfully with no errors, but columns that obviously contain SSNs aren't getting the SSN classification applied. Diagnose the likely cause, and what you'd check in the scan configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: A scan completing successfully with no errors only confirms that Purview was able to connect to the source and read its schema and sample data -- it says nothing about whether the right classification rules were actually included and executed during that scan. The most likely cause is that the scan rule set attached to this specific scan doesn't include the system classification rule for US Social Security Numbers, or a needed custom classification rule was never created and attached, meaning nothing was ever actually looking for that pattern while the scan ran. What to check: the exact scan rule set used for this scan (not just confirming that a scan ran), whether it includes the relevant system classification and whether that classification's confidence threshold or data sampling settings actually caught the real values present, and whether a custom classification is needed if the SSNs are stored in a nonstandard format the built-in system rule doesn't recognize (e.g., no dashes, or embedded in a composite field).
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd flag immediately is that 'the scan finished with no errors' and 'the right classifications were applied' are two completely separate claims -- a clean scan just means Purview successfully connected and read the schema, it doesn't mean the scan was actually looking for SSNs in the first place. My first check would be the scan rule set attached to this specific scan, because it's entirely possible someone created the scan with the default or a trimmed-down rule set that never included the SSN classification at all -- in which case the scan was never going to flag it, successful or not. If the SSN classification IS included in the rule set, my next check would be the data itself versus what the classifier expects -- if these SSNs are stored without dashes, or embedded inside a larger composite string field, the built-in system classification pattern might just not recognize that format, which would call for a custom classification rule tuned to the actual format in use. I'd also sanity check the sampling settings, since a classification can miss a column if the sample Purview pulled during the scan happened to land on a subset of rows that don't clearly show the pattern.
commonMistakes: Assuming a successful, error-free scan means the right classifications were applied
Not checking which specific scan rule set was actually attached to this scan
Overlooking that a nonstandard data format (no dashes, embedded in a composite field) can defeat the built-in system classification
Not considering that sampling settings could cause a classification to be missed on some columns
keyPoints: A scan completing without errors only confirms connectivity and schema read -- not that the right classifications ran
The scan rule set actually attached to the scan determines which classifications are checked
A nonstandard data format can defeat a built-in system classification, requiring a custom rule
Sampling settings can also cause a classification to be missed even when the right rule is included

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that a clean scan doesn't guarantee the right classifications ran
Correctly identifies checking the scan rule set as the primary diagnostic step
Identifies nonstandard data format as a plausible cause requiring a custom classification
Mentions sampling settings as an additional plausible factor

questions.title: Designing a Glossary Term Approval Workflow
questions.prompt: Design the end-to-end governance workflow for proposing, reviewing, and approving a new business glossary term at a mid-size company, from the moment someone requests a new term to the moment it's published for enterprise use. Name the roles involved and what each one is responsible for.
questions.modelAnswer: A workable workflow needs four distinct roles with clear, non-overlapping responsibilities. The requester -- any business user -- proposes a new term with a draft definition and context for why it's needed. A data steward reviews the submission for clarity and, critically, checks whether an overlapping or duplicate term already exists before it goes any further, then routes it to the right business owner. The business or domain owner -- the person actually accountable for that business area -- reviews and approves (or sends back for revision) the definition for accuracy and completeness; this role has to sit with the business, not IT, since the whole point is business-meaning accountability. A governance council or data governance committee exists to resolve disputes when a term spans multiple domains or when two proposed definitions conflict, acting as an escalation path rather than approving every routine term. The sequence: propose with a draft definition, steward review for duplication and clarity, owner approval, then publication by a catalog admin with versioning, so later changes are tracked rather than silently overwriting the approved definition.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this so no single person is both proposing and approving, and so routine terms don't all have to go through a full committee. Requester: anyone in the business can propose a term, with a draft definition attached -- I wouldn't gatekeep who's allowed to propose, since the goal is capturing real business vocabulary, not restricting who gets a voice. Data steward: first checkpoint, checking for duplicates or near-duplicates (a huge amount of glossary mess comes from the same concept getting proposed twice under different names) and making sure the draft is clear enough to actually review, then routing it to the right owner. Business/domain owner: this is the person who's accountable for that term meaning what it says it means going forward -- not IT, because IT can tell you how a column is implemented but can't tell you what the business actually means by the word. Governance council: I'd only route something here when there's a genuine dispute -- two owners both claiming the term, or a definition that conflicts with an existing related term -- not as a mandatory stop for every proposal, since that turns a two-day process into a six-week one. Publication is the last step, and it needs versioning baked in from day one, because a term's definition will get refined over time and silently overwriting history makes it impossible to understand why a report's numbers changed after a definition update.
commonMistakes: Designing a workflow where the same person or team both proposes and approves terms, with no independent review
Routing every single term through a full governance committee instead of reserving it for genuine disputes
Assigning business glossary ownership to IT instead of an accountable business/domain owner
Omitting versioning at publication, making it impossible to trace how and when a definition changed
keyPoints: Four distinct roles: requester, data steward, business/domain owner, governance council for disputes
The steward's duplicate/overlap check prevents the same concept being defined multiple times under different names
Business ownership belongs with the business, not IT, since it's about accountable meaning, not implementation
Published terms need versioning so definition changes are tracked, not silently overwritten

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a complete, logically ordered end-to-end workflow
Correctly assigns distinct roles and responsibilities, including business ownership
Includes a duplicate/overlap check and a dispute-resolution escalation path
Addresses versioning/change tracking at publication

questions.title: Designing How Glossary Terms Link to Physical Columns Across Three Systems
questions.prompt: Design how you'd structure the relationship between business glossary terms and the actual physical database columns that implement them, for an enterprise with the same concept (e.g. 'Customer Lifetime Value') implemented differently in three separate systems (CRM, ERP, and a data warehouse). What does the catalog need to capture for this to actually be useful?
questions.modelAnswer: The right structure is a many-to-many linking model, not a single term-to-column pointer: one glossary term -- 'Customer Lifetime Value' -- carries one governed definition, and it links to multiple technical assets across the three systems (a CRM field, an ERP computed attribute, and a warehouse fact table column), since the same business concept genuinely has multiple physical implementations. Each individual link needs to capture more than just 'this column implements this term' -- it needs a note on whether that specific implementation fully, partially, or only approximately satisfies the governed definition, since three independently built systems rarely compute something like lifetime value identically. The catalog should also designate, where one exists, which implementation is considered the system of record for reporting purposes, and capture ownership/steward information per linked asset so a discovered discrepancy between two implementations gets routed to the right people rather than becoming an unowned mystery.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd resist the urge to force a single clean one-to-one mapping here, because that's not actually the reality -- three systems built this independently and almost certainly compute it slightly differently, and pretending otherwise just hides the discrepancy instead of surfacing it. My design is a term with multiple linked technical assets, each link carrying its own metadata about how well that implementation actually matches the governed definition -- full match, partial match with a specific known difference, or approximate/legacy implementation that probably needs revisiting. I'd also want a clear answer, captured in the catalog itself, to 'if someone asks for Customer Lifetime Value for a report, which implementation should they actually use' -- designating a system of record where one genuinely exists, rather than leaving every consumer to guess or pick whichever one they already had access to. And every link needs an owner, because the value of capturing 'this implementation differs from the others in this specific way' evaporates if nobody's actually responsible for knowing about it or fixing it.
commonMistakes: Designing a single one-to-one term-to-column link when the reality is genuinely multiple differing implementations
Not capturing how well each specific implementation matches the governed definition (full/partial/approximate)
Failing to designate a system of record, leaving consumers to guess which implementation to actually use
Omitting ownership on each individual link, so a known discrepancy has nobody responsible for it
keyPoints: A many-to-many link model reflects the reality of multiple differing implementations of one governed term
Each link should capture how closely that implementation matches the governed definition
Designating a system of record (where one exists) resolves ambiguity for downstream consumers
Ownership per linked asset ensures known discrepancies are someone's responsibility to track or fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs a many-to-many term-to-asset linking structure
Captures how well each implementation matches the governed definition
Addresses designating a system of record for downstream consumers
Includes ownership/stewardship per linked asset
