questions.title: Designing an Impact-Analysis Gate for Schema Changes
questions.prompt: Design the process you'd put in place so that no DBA or developer can alter or drop a column on a shared production table without first understanding its downstream impact. What would actually have to happen before a change like that is allowed to go through?
questions.modelAnswer: The design is a mandatory impact-analysis gate embedded directly in the change management process, not a best-practice suggestion developers can skip under time pressure. Any DDL change touching a shared or governed table triggers a required step: querying the lineage tool or data map for every downstream consumer of that specific table/column. The resulting impact report -- listing every affected object and its owner -- must be attached to the change request itself before it can move to approval; a change ticket missing this attachment simply doesn't proceed. Sign-off requirements should scale with blast radius: a column used by one minor internal report needs lighter sign-off than one feeding fifteen financial reports. Because most organizations don't yet have this technically enforced inside the deployment pipeline itself, the gate is usually enforced procedurally -- as a mandatory checklist item in change approval or CAB review -- until tooling can enforce it automatically.
questions.professionalAnswer: The design principle I'd insist on is that this can't be a step people are trusted to remember to do -- it has to be a hard gate that the change process itself refuses to move past without. Concretely: any DDL change against a table on the governed/shared list requires the requester to run an impact query against the lineage tool first, and the actual output -- not a summary, the real list of affected objects and their owners -- gets attached to the change ticket. No attachment, no approval; that's a hard rule, not a suggestion. I'd scale the sign-off burden to the blast radius rather than treating every change identically -- a column feeding one low-traffic internal dashboard doesn't need the same ceremony as one fifteen finance reports depend on, or the process becomes so heavy people start finding ways around it. Since most places I've seen don't have this wired directly into their deployment tooling yet, I'd implement it as a required checklist item inside whatever change approval board or process already exists, with the expectation that it eventually becomes a technical gate rather than a procedural one as the tooling matures.
commonMistakes: Treating impact analysis as a best practice developers should remember rather than a hard, enforced gate
Not requiring the actual impact report to be attached to the change request before approval
Applying the same heavy sign-off process to every change regardless of how many downstream consumers are affected
Assuming this needs to be a fully automated pipeline gate from day one instead of starting as an enforced procedural checklist
keyPoints: The gate must be mandatory and enforced, not a best practice that can be skipped under pressure
The actual impact report, not a summary, must be attached to the change request before approval
Sign-off requirements should scale with the number and criticality of affected downstream consumers
A procedural (checklist/CAB) gate is a realistic starting point before full pipeline-level enforcement exists

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a mandatory, enforced gate rather than a best-practice suggestion
Requires the actual impact report attached to the change request as a hard precondition
Scales sign-off requirements to the blast radius of the change
Gives a realistic path to enforcement given most orgs lack full pipeline-level tooling

questions.title: Designing End-to-End Lineage Documentation for a Revenue Report
questions.prompt: Design how you'd document end-to-end lineage for an executive revenue report that pulls from a source OLTP database, through a nightly ETL job, into a warehouse fact table, and finally into a Power BI semantic model and dashboard. What needs to be captured at each hop, and who should own keeping it current?
questions.modelAnswer: Design the documentation per hop, since each one has a different owner and a different kind of transformation worth capturing. Source: the specific table and column, with the system owner identified. ETL: the actual transformation logic applied -- which joins, filters, and calculated fields -- plus the specific job or pipeline name, owned by data engineering. Warehouse: the fact or dimension table and column the data lands in, along with any further business-rule transformations applied at that layer (currency conversion, revenue recognition adjustments), since warehouse-layer logic often changes a figure's meaning in ways worth documenting explicitly. Semantic model: which warehouse column feeds which specific measure or column in the Power BI model, including any DAX calculation logic, owned by the BI/analytics team. Dashboard: which visual or report page actually surfaces that measure. No single person should own the entire chain end to end -- each hop's owner is responsible for keeping their own segment current, and an automated lineage tool (ideally one that can capture lineage from ETL tools and from Power BI directly, like Purview) should be the thing stitching the separately-owned segments into one coherent end-to-end view, rather than relying on one person maintaining a hand-drawn diagram of the whole chain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this as segmented ownership stitched together by tooling, because expecting one person to maintain an accurate end-to-end diagram across four different layers owned by different teams just doesn't survive contact with reality -- it goes stale the first time any one layer changes without that person finding out. Each hop gets documented by whoever actually owns it: the source system owner documents the originating table/column, data engineering documents the ETL job's actual transformation logic (not just 'data flows from A to B,' but which joins and calculated fields are actually involved), the warehouse layer gets documented with any additional business-rule transformations applied there specifically, since that's often where a number's real meaning gets adjusted, and the BI team documents the semantic model's mapping from warehouse column to measure, including the DAX if there's calculation logic beyond a direct pass-through. What stitches these independently-maintained segments into one real end-to-end lineage view is tooling -- ideally something like Purview that can pull lineage directly from ADF/ETL tooling and from Power BI itself -- rather than hoping everyone's separately-documented segment happens to line up and stay in sync by coincidence.
commonMistakes: Assigning end-to-end lineage documentation to a single owner instead of segmenting it by the team that actually owns each hop
Documenting only 'Table A feeds Table B' at each hop instead of the actual transformation logic applied
Omitting warehouse-layer business-rule transformations, which often change a figure's real meaning
Relying entirely on manually maintained diagrams instead of using tooling to stitch segments together automatically where possible
keyPoints: Each hop (source, ETL, warehouse, semantic model, dashboard) should be documented by its actual owner
Transformation logic, not just 'this feeds that,' needs to be captured at the ETL and warehouse hops specifically
No single person should be expected to own accurate end-to-end lineage across teams they don't work on
Automated lineage tooling should stitch independently-maintained segments into one coherent view

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly specifies what needs documenting at each of the five hops
Correctly assigns ownership of each segment to the team that actually owns it
Recognizes transformation logic, not just flow direction, needs capturing
Proposes tooling to stitch segments together rather than relying on one person

questions.title: Choosing an MDM Architecture Style for a Multi-System Customer Master
questions.prompt: A company has customer data duplicated and inconsistent across three systems (CRM, e-commerce platform, and billing). Design which MDM architecture style -- registry, consolidation, coexistence, or centralized -- you'd recommend, and explain the tradeoff that led you there.
questions.modelAnswer: Walking through the styles: registry style keeps the actual data in the source systems and maintains only a cross-reference index of matching IDs plus a thin set of consolidated attributes -- lowest implementation cost and disruption, but the resulting golden record is shallow and lives distributed across sources rather than as a real, queryable consolidated record. Consolidation style builds a genuinely complete golden record in a separate MDM hub by pulling and merging data from all three sources, typically used for analytics and reporting rather than being written back to by source systems. Coexistence style goes further, synchronizing the consolidated golden record back out to the source systems so everyone stays current, at the cost of real integration investment. Centralized/transactional style makes the hub itself the actual system of entry going forward, requiring the most disruption to existing workflows. The recommendation depends on the actual goal: if this is fundamentally about getting accurate reporting and analytics without disrupting how CRM, e-commerce, and billing teams currently work, consolidation is the pragmatic choice; if billing specifically needs to stop billing a now-merged duplicate separately, coexistence is justified despite higher cost, since consolidation alone wouldn't fix that operational problem; registry is reasonable only as a fast, low-budget first step.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this by first asking what the actual pain point is, because the right style really does depend on it. If I just need accurate reporting -- one trustworthy view of customers for analytics without touching how CRM, e-commerce, and billing teams operate day to day -- consolidation is the sweet spot: build a real, complete golden record in an MDM hub by merging the three sources, and let reporting consume that instead of each system's own messy version. But if the actual complaint includes something operational, like billing still charging a duplicate customer twice because billing itself never sees the corrected, merged view, consolidation alone doesn't solve that -- the golden record needs to flow back out to billing, which means coexistence, with the real integration cost that comes with it. Registry style I'd only recommend as a deliberately cheap, fast first step if there's no budget yet for a real MDM build -- it gives a lightweight cross-reference without committing to a full consolidated record, but it's a stopgap, not a destination. Centralized/transactional is the heaviest lift, making the hub the actual system of entry, and I'd only reach for that if the organization is ready for that level of workflow change, which three mid-size systems with existing processes usually aren't, at least not as a first move.
commonMistakes: Recommending a style without first clarifying whether the actual need is reporting-only or also operational correction
Recommending centralized/transactional as a default without acknowledging the major workflow disruption it requires
Not distinguishing registry's thin cross-reference from consolidation's genuinely complete golden record
Treating all four styles as roughly interchangeable instead of tying the choice to a specific tradeoff
keyPoints: Registry: lowest cost, thin cross-reference, data stays in source systems
Consolidation: a real, complete golden record in a hub, typically for reporting/analytics
Coexistence: consolidation plus syncing the golden record back to source systems for operational correction
Centralized/transactional: the hub becomes the actual system of entry, highest disruption

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the tradeoffs of at least three of the four architecture styles
Ties the recommendation to a specific, named constraint (reporting-only vs. operational)
Explains why consolidation alone is insufficient if billing needs operational correction
Gives a clear, defensible recommendation rather than listing options with no conclusion

questions.title: Designing Survivorship and Hierarchy Rules for a Product Master
questions.prompt: Design the survivorship rules and hierarchy structure for a Product master that needs to reconcile product data coming from an ERP system (authoritative for cost and supplier) and an e-commerce platform (authoritative for description, images, and customer-facing category). How do hierarchies factor into this beyond just field-level survivorship?
questions.modelAnswer: The survivorship design should be field-level, with a designated trusted source per attribute rather than one blanket rule applied to the whole record: cost, supplier, and SKU-level attributes survive from ERP, while description, images, and marketing category survive from the e-commerce platform -- effectively a per-field trusted-source table, since recency alone doesn't reflect which system is actually authoritative for a given attribute. Hierarchies add a second, separate dimension: products also belong to category hierarchies, and ERP's internal commodity classification is very likely a genuinely different hierarchy from e-commerce's customer-facing category tree, built for different purposes (procurement/accounting versus browsing/merchandising). The design shouldn't force one hierarchy to serve both purposes -- the product master needs to maintain both hierarchies as distinct, explicitly maintained structures, with a defined mapping between an ERP commodity code and its corresponding customer-facing category, so that reporting can roll up correctly whichever hierarchy the report actually needs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build the survivorship rules around a simple principle: trust the system that's actually authoritative for that specific attribute, not the system that happens to be most recently updated or most complete overall. So cost, supplier, SKU details -- ERP wins, full stop, because that's genuinely where that data is managed and accurate. Description, images, customer-facing category -- e-commerce wins, because that's the system actually built for presenting the product to customers. I'd implement that as an explicit per-field trusted-source table rather than a single rule, because a blanket 'most recent wins' rule would occasionally let an e-commerce team's casual edit to a cost field (if they even have write access to it) override ERP's accurate figure. The hierarchy piece is where I'd push back if someone suggested just picking one category tree -- ERP's commodity classification exists for procurement and accounting rollups, and e-commerce's category tree exists for how customers actually browse, and those are legitimately different structures serving different audiences. Rather than compromising on one hierarchy that serves neither purpose well, I'd maintain both explicitly in the product master, with a clear mapping table connecting an ERP commodity code to its corresponding customer-facing category, so any report can roll up correctly through whichever hierarchy actually matches the question being asked.
commonMistakes: Applying a single blanket survivorship rule (e.g. most recent wins) instead of a per-field trusted-source design
Letting the e-commerce platform's data win for attributes like cost or supplier it was never meant to manage
Forcing ERP's commodity hierarchy and e-commerce's category hierarchy into a single shared structure
Not maintaining an explicit mapping between the two hierarchies, breaking rollups that need to cross between them
keyPoints: Survivorship should be field-level, with a designated trusted source per attribute, not one blanket rule
ERP and e-commerce are each authoritative for different attributes based on what they actually manage
Product category hierarchies often genuinely differ by purpose (procurement vs. customer browsing) and shouldn't be merged into one
An explicit mapping between the two hierarchies is needed for correct cross-purpose reporting rollups

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs field-level survivorship with the correct trusted source per attribute
Correctly explains why a blanket survivorship rule is the wrong design here
Recognizes the two hierarchies serve different purposes and shouldn't be merged
Proposes an explicit mapping between the two hierarchies

questions.title: Designing an Access Governance Model for a PII-Containing Finance Warehouse
questions.prompt: Design an access governance model for a finance data warehouse that contains customer PII, covering roles, least privilege, and segregation of duties. Who should be able to see what, and what would you explicitly prevent any single role from being able to do alone?
questions.modelAnswer: Design a tiered role structure: a read-only reporting role sees masked PII by default and aggregate-level finance figures, with no row-level detail beyond what's genuinely needed; a finance analyst role has unmasked access, but scoped to only the specific accounts or regions they own, enforced via row-level security rather than warehouse-wide access; a data steward/governance role can view classification and lineage metadata but generally not the underlying masked values themselves; and a narrow, time-boxed privileged-access role exists specifically for PII unmasking tied to a documented investigation, rather than standing access anyone keeps indefinitely. Least privilege means every new role defaults to the most restrictive access that's still useful, with any broader grant requiring explicit justification, rather than defaulting broad and trimming later, which rarely actually happens. Segregation of duties means explicitly preventing any single role from both approving its own access grants and holding those same grants (no self-approval), and preventing the same role from both unmasking PII and exporting/extracting data unsupervised -- these specific combinations should require two different people, or at minimum a documented secondary approval, so no one person can quietly both grant themselves access and use it without anyone else knowing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design the roles around how much of the data someone genuinely needs to see, not around organizational title. A read-only reporting role gets masked PII and aggregate figures -- that covers the majority of people who just need the numbers, not the identities behind them. A finance analyst gets real, unmasked access, but only to the specific slice of accounts or regions they're actually responsible for, enforced with row-level security so 'finance analyst' doesn't quietly mean 'sees every customer in the warehouse.' Governance and stewardship roles see metadata -- classifications, lineage, who owns what -- without needing the actual masked values most of the time. And then there's a genuinely narrow privileged role for actual unmasking, which I'd make time-boxed and tied to a specific documented reason, not a standing grant anyone just keeps forever once they've had it once. The segregation-of-duties piece I'd be strict about: nobody self-approves their own access -- that's a hard rule, not a guideline -- and I'd never let the same role both unmask PII and freely export data without a second person in the loop, because that single combination is exactly how a PII leak happens quietly, with no second set of eyes anywhere in the process.
commonMistakes: Designing roles around job titles rather than the actual minimum access each function genuinely needs
Granting finance analysts warehouse-wide unmasked access instead of scoping via row-level security
Treating privileged unmask access as a standing grant instead of time-boxed and tied to a specific reason
Not explicitly preventing self-approval of access or the single-role combination of unmasking plus unsupervised export
keyPoints: Roles should be tiered by actual need: masked/aggregate by default, unmasked only where genuinely required and scoped
Row-level security should scope even privileged roles to only the data they're responsible for
Least privilege means defaulting to the most restrictive useful access, not defaulting broad and trimming later
Segregation of duties explicitly blocks self-approval and the unmask-plus-unsupervised-export combination in one role

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sensible tiered role structure matching access to genuine need
Correctly applies least privilege as a default-restrictive principle
Specifies concrete segregation-of-duties rules, including self-approval and unmask-plus-export
Addresses row-level scoping even for privileged/analyst roles

questions.title: Designing a Classification and Masking Strategy for a New PII Data Lake
questions.prompt: Design the classification and protection strategy for a new data lake that will ingest PII from five different source systems (HR, CRM, e-commerce, support tickets, and marketing). What needs to happen before a single row lands, and what protects the data once it's there?
questions.modelAnswer: Before ingestion, define a classification scheme upfront -- for example Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted, with PII specifically flagged within the more sensitive tiers -- and require every new source to go through a classification review identifying which specific columns are PII before they're mapped into the lake, rather than classifying reactively after the fact. Establish consistent tagging/naming conventions so classified columns are discoverable immediately once scanned (via a tool like Purview applying classification rules during ingestion scans). Once data is landing, apply masking or tokenization to PII columns by default in every layer except a tightly restricted raw/bronze zone used only for initial ingestion; encrypt data at rest and in transit as a baseline, independent of masking; apply row- and column-level security so each consumer role only sees the subset actually relevant to them; and ensure the lake's overall access model follows least privilege rather than defaulting to broad lake-wide visibility. The key design principle: classification has to happen at or before ingestion, not as a cleanup pass afterward, because once PII has already propagated into multiple downstream derived datasets, protecting it everywhere it has spread becomes substantially harder than preventing the spread in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: The design decision I'd be most insistent on is doing classification before data lands, not after. Five source systems means five separate onboarding reviews, each one identifying exactly which columns are PII in that specific source before anything gets mapped into the lake -- if I let that slip to 'we'll classify it once it's in,' by the time anyone gets around to it, that PII has likely already been copied into two or three derived datasets, and now I'm chasing it across the lake instead of controlling it at the door. Once the classification scheme exists -- something like Public/Internal/Confidential/Restricted with PII flagged specifically -- I'd apply masking or tokenization by default to any PII column outside a narrowly scoped raw ingestion zone, encrypt everything at rest and in transit as a non-negotiable baseline, and use row/column-level security so, say, marketing sees only what marketing actually needs rather than a wide-open view of five systems' worth of combined customer data. I'd also lean on tooling like Purview to apply and verify classification automatically during scanning, since relying on five different source teams to manually tag their own PII consistently is asking for gaps.
commonMistakes: Classifying data reactively after ingestion instead of reviewing each source for PII before it's mapped into the lake
Applying masking only in reporting layers while leaving PII fully exposed in raw/bronze with no compensating controls
Granting broad lake-wide access by default instead of scoping each consumer to what they actually need
Relying on manual tagging across five separate source teams instead of automated classification tooling during ingestion
keyPoints: Classification review must happen per source before ingestion, not as a reactive cleanup afterward
Masking/tokenization should be the default for PII outside a narrowly scoped raw ingestion zone
Encryption at rest and in transit is a baseline control independent of masking
Access should follow least privilege via row/column-level security, not broad default lake-wide visibility

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly emphasizes classification before ingestion rather than reactive cleanup
Designs concrete protection controls (masking, encryption, row/column security)
Applies least privilege to the overall access model
Mentions tooling (e.g. automated classification/scanning) to make this scale across five sources

questions.title: Designing Collections and Domains for a Multi-Business-Unit Enterprise
questions.prompt: Design the Collections and domain structure in Microsoft Purview for an enterprise with three largely independent business units, each with its own data sources and data stewards, but a shared enterprise governance team that needs visibility across all three. What boundaries and roles would you set up?
questions.modelAnswer: Design a Collections hierarchy that mirrors the actual org structure: a root collection owned by the enterprise governance team, with broad read visibility across everything registered beneath it, and a child collection per business unit, each scoped so that business unit's stewards have full management permissions within their own collection but no access into the other business units' collections. Register each business unit's own data sources into their respective child collection, so scans and the resulting discovered assets stay scoped there rather than mixing across units. Role assignment: collection admins at each business unit level manage their own sources and scans; data curators within each collection can edit asset descriptions and glossary links scoped to that collection; data readers assigned at the enterprise/root level can see across all three business units for oversight and enterprise-wide reporting, without having permission to modify any individual business unit's assets. This structure gives each business unit real autonomy over its own data and stewardship while still letting the enterprise governance team see and report across the whole estate from the root.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build the Collections hierarchy to mirror the actual organizational boundaries rather than a generic structure, because the whole point here is that these three business units are largely independent and should stay that way operationally, while still being visible to the center. Root collection: owned and administered by the enterprise governance team, with read access cascading down into everything beneath it, but I wouldn't give the root team edit rights into each business unit's assets by default -- visibility and control are different things, and I'd keep them separate. Each business unit gets its own child collection, registers its own sources into it, and its own stewards get full collection-admin rights scoped to just that collection -- they can manage their sources, run their scans, curate their assets, without needing anyone's permission from the other two units or stepping on each other. The enterprise governance team's actual role here is a data-reader role assigned at the root, which inherits visibility down into every child collection for reporting and oversight purposes, without granting them the ability to edit or break anything inside a business unit's own scope. That split -- read-everywhere at the top, manage-only-your-own at the business unit level -- is what actually makes both halves of the requirement work at once.
commonMistakes: Designing a flat, single collection instead of a hierarchy that mirrors the actual organizational boundaries
Giving the enterprise governance team edit/manage rights into each business unit's collection instead of read-only oversight
Not scoping each business unit's stewards to only their own collection, allowing cross-unit interference
Registering all sources into one shared collection instead of scoping each business unit's sources to their own child collection
keyPoints: A Collections hierarchy should mirror the organization's actual boundaries: root plus one child per business unit
Each business unit's stewards get full management scoped to their own collection only
Enterprise governance gets read visibility across all collections from the root, not edit rights into each unit
Sources should be registered into the business unit's own collection to keep scans and assets properly scoped

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs a hierarchical Collections structure mirroring the org boundaries
Correctly scopes each business unit's steward permissions to their own collection
Correctly gives enterprise governance read-only cross-unit visibility, not edit rights
Addresses where each business unit's sources should be registered

questions.title: Designing How Purview Lineage Supports Impact Analysis Across ADF and Power BI
questions.prompt: Design how you'd use Microsoft Purview's lineage capabilities to support impact analysis for a pipeline that moves data via Azure Data Factory into Synapse, and then into Power BI reports. What does Purview capture automatically versus what you'd still need to document manually?
questions.modelAnswer: The design registers ADF, Synapse, and the Power BI tenant as scanned or connected sources, so Purview automatically captures lineage edges for ADF activities -- copy and data flow activities generate lineage between their source and sink datasets -- and for Power BI, where datasets and dataflows connect to their underlying sources, down to report and dashboard level in supported scenarios. This produces an automatically maintained lineage graph running from source table, through the ADF pipeline, into the Synapse table, into the Power BI dataset, and on to the report, which Purview's impact analysis and lineage view can traverse directly. What's not automatically captured: business-rule-level detail buried inside complex transformation logic -- a stored procedure or an intricate data flow's exact column-level mapping may not be fully parsed depending on connector support -- and any business context, like why a dataset matters or who to contact about it, which still needs to be manually documented through descriptions, ownership fields, and business glossary term links attached to the relevant assets. The design treats Purview's automated lineage as the structural skeleton of the impact analysis, with manual curation filling in the business meaning on top of it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set this up by registering every hop as a scanned or connected source in Purview -- ADF, Synapse, and the Power BI workspace -- specifically because that's what lets Purview build the lineage graph automatically rather than me drawing it by hand. ADF's copy and data flow activities generate real lineage edges between their source and sink datasets on their own once registered, and Power BI's own lineage view connects datasets back to their underlying sources, which Purview can pick up too. End to end, that gives me a lineage chain I didn't have to manually maintain -- source table, through the pipeline, into Synapse, into the Power BI dataset, into the actual report -- and I can use that directly for impact analysis when someone wants to change something upstream. Where I'd stop trusting the automation completely is anything with real transformation complexity buried inside it -- if there's a gnarly stored procedure or a data flow with a lot of conditional logic, Purview's column-level lineage parsing might not capture the exact mapping perfectly, and I wouldn't claim it does without actually verifying it against the real logic. And no tool is going to tell me why a given report matters to the business or who to call about it -- that context still has to be manually added as descriptions, ownership, and glossary links on top of whatever lineage gets captured automatically.
commonMistakes: Assuming Purview captures full lineage automatically without registering each hop (ADF, Synapse, Power BI) as a connected source
Overstating confidence in column-level lineage accuracy for complex transformation logic without verifying it
Assuming automated lineage alone provides business context like ownership or why an asset matters
Treating the lineage graph as complete without checking which connectors actually support the needed level of detail
keyPoints: Registering ADF, Synapse, and Power BI as scanned/connected sources is what enables automatic lineage capture
ADF activities and Power BI's own source connections generate lineage edges automatically once registered
Complex transformation logic may not be fully parsed at column-level depending on connector support
Business context (ownership, descriptions, glossary links) must still be added manually on top of automated lineage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs source registration enabling automated lineage capture across all three hops
Correctly explains what Purview captures automatically at each hop
Correctly identifies the limits of automated column-level lineage for complex logic
Identifies business context as something that still requires manual curation

questions.title: A stakeholder wants a new field added mid-sprint
questions.prompt: Your team is three days into a two-week sprint when a stakeholder asks you to add a new field to a report you're already building, saying it's 'quick, shouldn't change anything.' Walk me through how you'd actually handle this request.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just say yes or no -- it describes a specific process for evaluating a mid-sprint request honestly before committing to it. First, actually assess the request rather than taking 'quick' at face value: does the new field require touching the dataset's underlying query, does it interact with existing filters or parameters, does it need its own testing? Second, be transparent with the stakeholder and the team about the real tradeoff: if it genuinely is small, say so and fold it in; if it's not, explain specifically why (not vaguely) and present the actual options -- add it now and risk the sprint's committed work, or add it to the next sprint, or (if it's urgent) swap it in for something already committed and explicitly deprioritized. The point to get across is that this isn't about being rigid or unhelpful -- it's about making the tradeoff visible instead of silently absorbing scope and then explaining later why other committed work slipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just say yes because it's described as quick, and I also wouldn't flatly refuse because 'that's not what we committed to' -- I'd actually go look at what the change requires first. If it really is a one-column addition to an existing dataset with no filter interactions, I'd just do it and move on, because treating every tiny request as a formal change-control event is its own kind of overhead. But if it touches the dataset's query, interacts with parameters already in play, or needs real testing, I'd say that specifically and honestly, rather than agreeing and then quietly having something else slip. I'd lay out the actual choice for the stakeholder and my Product Owner: we can add this now and something else committed to this sprint moves to next sprint, or this goes into the next sprint's backlog, or if it's genuinely urgent, I'll tell you specifically what I'd need to drop to make room for it. What I'm protecting isn't my own workload -- it's the team's ability to make an honest commitment and actually hit it, instead of everyone quietly absorbing 'just one more small thing' until the sprint's real scope bears no resemblance to what was planned.
commonMistakes: Automatically agreeing to the request without actually assessing its real scope first
Refusing rigidly without explaining the real tradeoff or offering alternatives
Silently absorbing the extra work and letting already-committed work slip without telling anyone why
Not involving the Product Owner or team in the actual tradeoff decision
keyPoints: Actually assesses the request's real scope instead of taking 'quick' at face value
Is transparent about the tradeoff rather than silently absorbing scope creep
Presents concrete options (do it now and drop something, defer it, or swap priorities)
Frames the goal as protecting the team's ability to make honest commitments, not personal workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes actually assessing the request's real scope rather than assuming
Shows transparent communication about the tradeoff involved
Presents concrete, realistic options rather than a flat yes/no
Frames this as protecting the team's commitments, not personal convenience

questions.title: Communicating a blocker in the daily standup
questions.prompt: You're stuck on a task -- a stored procedure change you need is waiting on another team's approval -- and it's been blocked for two days. How would you bring this up in the daily standup, and what would you do about it outside of standup?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the Daily Scrum correctly -- as a short team sync, not a status report to a manager -- and keeps the standup update itself brief and specific: what's blocked, who or what it's waiting on, and how long it's been stuck, rather than a long explanation of the underlying technical problem. The real work happens outside standup: actually escalating the blocker rather than just mentioning it and waiting -- following up directly with whoever owns the approval, looping in the Scrum Master if the blocker is specifically the kind of cross-team obstacle they're meant to help clear, and being honest with the team about the sprint-goal impact if it stays stuck much longer, rather than quietly hoping it resolves itself. The key distinction a strong answer draws is between mentioning a blocker (passive) and actively working to clear it (what's actually expected).
questions.professionalAnswer: In standup itself, I'd keep it tight: 'I'm blocked on the stored procedure change -- it's been waiting on sign-off from the other team for two days now, and I don't have a resolution plan yet.' That's it -- standup isn't the place to walk through the technical details or vent about how annoying the wait is; it's a quick sync so the team knows where things stand. The actual work happens right after standup, not during it. I'd go directly to whoever on the other team owns that approval and ask specifically what's holding it up and when I can expect it, rather than just waiting passively for two more days. If that doesn't move things, I'd loop in my Scrum Master specifically, because clearing exactly this kind of cross-team blocker is their job, not something I should be expected to just push through alone. And if it looks like this is going to threaten the sprint goal, I'd say that out loud to the team well before the sprint review, not as a surprise at the end -- being blocked isn't a failure on my part, but sitting on it quietly without escalating would be.
commonMistakes: Treating the standup as the place to explain the full technical backstory instead of a brief status
Mentioning the blocker in standup but then passively waiting instead of actively escalating it afterward
Not involving the Scrum Master, whose job specifically includes clearing cross-team blockers
Waiting until the sprint review to surface that the blocker threatened the sprint goal
keyPoints: The Daily Scrum update should be brief and specific, not a technical deep dive
Mentioning a blocker in standup isn't the same as actively working to clear it
Escalating directly to the other team and/or the Scrum Master is the appropriate next step
Sprint-goal risk should be surfaced early, not held until the sprint review

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes an appropriately brief, specific standup update
Describes actively escalating the blocker outside of standup, not just waiting
Correctly involves the Scrum Master's actual role in clearing blockers
Shows early, honest communication about sprint-goal risk

questions.title: Two stakeholders both want their ticket done first
questions.prompt: You have two open tickets: a bug fix a sales manager is pushing for urgently, and a new report feature your own manager assigned last week with a deadline that's actually sooner. Both stakeholders think their request is the priority. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't unilaterally decide between two stakeholders' competing priorities on its own authority -- it recognizes that prioritization decisions belong with whoever actually owns the backlog's priority order (a Product Owner, in Scrum terms, or whoever plays that role on the team), and surfaces the conflict to them explicitly rather than quietly picking one and hoping the other doesn't notice. The practical first step is gathering the actual facts needed to make the decision -- how urgent is the bug really (is it actively breaking something for users right now, or just annoying), and what's the real deadline and consequence of missing it for the report feature -- rather than just taking either stakeholder's framing of urgency at face value. Then bring both pieces of information to whoever should decide, make the conflict and the tradeoff explicit, and get an actual decision rather than silently deprioritizing one person's request without them knowing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't try to quietly referee this myself between two people who each think their thing is most important -- that's not actually my call to make alone, and if I just pick one, I've effectively made a business priority decision without the authority or the full context to make it well. My first step is getting the real facts: is this bug actually breaking something in production right now, or is it an annoyance that feels urgent but isn't actually blocking anyone? What's the real, hard deadline on the report feature, and what actually happens if it slips a few days? Once I have real answers instead of just each stakeholder's own sense of urgency, I'd go to whoever actually owns prioritization for my work -- my manager, or a Product Owner if that's how the team is structured -- lay out both asks and their actual urgency side by side, and ask for an explicit call. I'd rather spend ten minutes getting a clear decision than spend a day guessing which stakeholder to disappoint and then having to explain that choice after the fact.
commonMistakes: Unilaterally deciding between two stakeholders' competing priorities without the authority or full context to do so
Taking either stakeholder's self-reported urgency at face value instead of verifying the actual impact and deadline
Quietly deprioritizing one request without telling that stakeholder, letting them find out later
Not escalating to whoever actually owns prioritization decisions for the team's work
keyPoints: Prioritization conflicts between stakeholders should be escalated, not unilaterally resolved
Gathers real facts about urgency and deadlines rather than accepting either framing at face value
Brings both pieces of information to whoever owns the priority decision for an explicit call
Avoids silently deprioritizing a stakeholder without their knowledge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes this isn't a unilateral decision and escalates appropriately
Describes gathering real facts about urgency/impact before escalating
Describes a clear, explicit escalation with both pieces of information presented
Avoids silently disappointing either stakeholder without communication

questions.title: A ticket has no acceptance criteria
questions.prompt: You pick up a ticket from the sprint backlog that says 'Add a filter for region to the sales dashboard' with no further detail -- no acceptance criteria, no mention of default behavior or how it should interact with existing filters. What do you do before writing any code?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the temptation to just start building based on a guess, because a story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done -- 'I think this is done' and a shared, checkable definition of done are different things, and building against the wrong assumption wastes real time for both the developer and whoever has to send it back. The right move is going back to whoever owns the ticket -- the Product Owner or the stakeholder who requested it -- and asking specific, concrete questions rather than one vague 'what do you mean': what should the filter's default value be, does it need to interact with (cascade from or into) any existing filters already on the dashboard, and is there a specific list of regions or should it reflect whatever's in the data. Writing those answers down as explicit acceptance criteria before starting, not after, turns a vague request into something both the developer and whoever reviews the finished work can actually check against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start building off a guess, because 'add a filter for region' sounds simple but actually hides several real decisions -- what region data source is sensible as the dropdown's default, whether this filter needs to interact with any filter already on the dashboard, whether 'region' even means the same thing across every table the dashboard touches. Guessing wrong on any of those means I build something, it gets reviewed, and it comes back with changes -- which is slower overall than just asking upfront. So before writing anything, I'd go back to whoever owns the ticket with specific questions, not a vague 'can you clarify this' -- I'd ask directly: should this default to the viewer's own region if we track that, does selecting a region need to affect any other filter already on the page, and is there an existing region list I should match or is this open-ended. Once I have real answers, I'd write them down as the ticket's acceptance criteria myself if nobody else does, specifically so there's a shared, checkable definition everyone agrees to before I start -- that protects me too, since I now have something concrete to point back to if the request changes later.
commonMistakes: Starting to build based on a guess instead of clarifying ambiguous requirements first
Asking a vague 'can you clarify this ticket' instead of specific, concrete questions
Not writing down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting
Assuming the ticket's brevity means the request is actually simple, missing the real decisions hidden inside it
keyPoints: A story without acceptance criteria is genuinely too vague to know when it's actually done
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request for more detail
Writes down the clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria before starting work
Clarifying upfront is faster overall than building on a guess and having it sent back

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes the ticket is too ambiguous to build from directly
Asks specific, concrete clarifying questions rather than a vague request
Describes writing down clarified requirements as explicit acceptance criteria
Explains why clarifying upfront saves time overall

questions.title: The Business Says the Dashboard You Built Isn't What They Asked For
questions.prompt: You finish a dashboard, it passes your own testing, and then the business stakeholder reviews it in UAT and says it doesn't actually answer what they needed. How do you respond, and how do you prevent the same gap next time?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats a UAT rejection as a normal, expected signal rather than a personal failure or a sign the stakeholder is being difficult — UAT exists specifically to catch the case where code is technically correct but isn't actually what the business needed, which is a different question than QA's "does it work correctly" entirely. The right immediate response is to ask specific, concrete questions rather than getting defensive: what exactly does the current version show, what were they expecting instead, and can they point to a specific number or view that's wrong relative to their mental model. Often the real gap traces back to acceptance criteria that were vague or incomplete at the start, not a build mistake — which is the actual thing to fix going forward: writing more specific, checkable acceptance criteria during intake (edge cases included, like what a zero-sales region should display) so UAT becomes a confirmation step rather than where requirements gaps first surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is not get defensive about it, because UAT rejecting something isn't the same as me having done something wrong — it's literally what that stage is for, catching the gap between 'this is technically correct' and 'this is actually what we needed,' which are genuinely different questions. I'd ask specific questions rather than just apologizing and reworking blindly: what exactly were you expecting to see here, can you show me a specific number that looks wrong to you versus what you expected. Usually when I dig into it, the real root cause isn't that I built the wrong thing technically — it's that the original request or acceptance criteria were vague enough that I made a reasonable assumption that just wasn't the assumption they were making. Going forward, the actual fix isn't 'be more careful next time,' it's writing tighter, more specific acceptance criteria up front — including the edge cases, like what happens when a region has zero sales for the month — so that gap gets caught during planning instead of surfacing for the first time in UAT.
commonMistakes: Treating a UAT rejection as a personal failure or getting defensive instead of investigating specifically
Reworking the dashboard based on a vague complaint without asking specific clarifying questions first
Not tracing the root cause back to incomplete acceptance criteria, repeating the same gap on the next project
Assuming the stakeholder is simply wrong instead of taking their feedback as a genuine signal about the request
keyPoints: UAT exists specifically to catch 'technically correct but not what was needed,' a different question than QA
The right response is specific clarifying questions, not defensiveness or blind rework
The root cause is often vague acceptance criteria at intake, not a build mistake
The real fix is tighter acceptance criteria going forward, including edge cases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds professionally and non-defensively to the rejection
Describes asking specific clarifying questions
Correctly identifies the likely root cause (acceptance criteria gap)
Proposes a concrete prevention for next time

questions.title: A Dashboard Goes Live, and Immediately Something's Wrong
questions.prompt: Two days after a new regional revenue dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region, which is obviously wrong. Walk through how you'd investigate this and what you'd communicate to the regional manager while you're still figuring it out.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the investigation from the communication, and gets both moving in parallel rather than going silent until the fix is found. On investigation, the logical order is checking the environments closest to the symptom first: is this specific region's data actually present in the underlying source as of the relevant date, did the scheduled refresh for this model actually complete successfully (checking refresh history for errors), and does any report-level filter (RLS, a regional filter default) unintentionally exclude this region's rows. On communication, the mistake to avoid is going quiet until the root cause is fully found — the right move is an immediate, honest acknowledgment that specifically names what's being checked ("I've confirmed the issue and I'm checking whether it's a refresh failure or a filter problem, I'll update you within the hour") rather than either a vague "looking into it" or disappearing until there's a complete answer, since a specific update lets the regional manager decide what to do in the meantime (for example, whether to trust other numbers from the same report).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd do two things essentially at the same time: start investigating, and send the regional manager something specific right away rather than going quiet until I have a full answer. On the investigation side, I'd work from the symptom outward — first checking refresh history to see whether last night's scheduled refresh for this model actually succeeded, since a failed or partial refresh is a really common cause of 'this one region looks wrong.' If the refresh is fine, I'd check whether the region's data is actually present in the source table for the relevant date, and then check whether any filter — RLS, a default slicer, anything report-level — is quietly excluding that region specifically. On the communication side, I'd send something concrete almost immediately, like 'I've confirmed something's wrong with the regional number, I'm checking whether it's a refresh issue or a filter issue right now, I'll have an update for you within the hour' — specific enough that they know I've actually looked at it and know roughly when to expect more, rather than a vague 'we're on it' that tells them nothing.
commonMistakes: Going silent until the root cause is fully found instead of sending a specific interim update
Guessing at the cause instead of checking refresh history and filters methodically
Sending a vague 'we're looking into it' instead of naming what's specifically being checked
Fixing the symptom without identifying why it happened, risking a repeat next refresh cycle
keyPoints: Investigation and communication should happen in parallel, not sequentially
A methodical check order: refresh history, source data presence, then report-level filters
A specific interim update is far more useful than a vague one or silence
The regional manager should know roughly when to expect a further update

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a methodical, logically ordered investigation
Describes a specific, honest interim communication, not silence or vagueness
Recognizes investigation and communication should happen together
Mentions follow-up to prevent recurrence

questions.title: A Stakeholder Disputes Your Data Quality Finding
questions.prompt: You report that 12% of orders in a feed have invalid ship dates. The business stakeholder responds, 'Your check must be wrong, we'd know if that many orders were broken.' How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't get defensive about the finding, and doesn't quietly back down just because the stakeholder pushed back confidently either -- it treats the pushback as a reasonable request for evidence and responds by actually showing the work rather than restating the conclusion more firmly. The right move is sharing the specific rule the check used to define 'invalid' (for example, ship date earlier than order date, or a NULL ship date), pulling a handful of concrete example rows the stakeholder can independently look up and verify themselves, and inviting them to check a sample directly rather than just asking them to trust the number. A strong answer recognizes there are genuinely two possibilities here -- the check itself could be wrong (bad logic, a misread date format, a timezone issue), or the stakeholder's mental model of the data could be outdated -- and the way to find out which one it is is evidence, not confidence on either side.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't dig in and just repeat the number more firmly, and I wouldn't cave and quietly walk it back either -- both of those skip the actual step that resolves this, which is showing the work. I'd pull up ten real example order rows that failed the check, with the actual ship date and order date values visible, and hand those over directly so the stakeholder can verify them in the source system themselves rather than taking my word for a percentage. I'd also just say plainly what the rule was -- 'invalid means ship date is before order date, or ship date is null' -- because sometimes the disagreement isn't really about the data at all, it's that my definition of 'invalid' doesn't match what they assumed it meant. If the examples hold up, the conversation moves from 'your check is wrong' to 'okay, that's a real problem, let's find out why' -- which is a much more useful place to land than either of us just repeating our initial position with more confidence.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive and simply restating the percentage more firmly instead of showing concrete evidence
Backing down and assuming the check must be wrong just because the stakeholder pushed back confidently
Not sharing the exact rule used to define 'invalid,' leaving room for a definitional misunderstanding to go unresolved
Presenting only the aggregate percentage instead of concrete example rows the stakeholder can independently verify
keyPoints: Pushback on a data quality finding should be met with evidence, not firmer assertion or quiet retreat
Sharing the exact rule used and concrete example rows lets the stakeholder verify independently
The disagreement might be about the data, or it might be a definitional mismatch about what 'invalid' means
The goal is resolving via evidence, moving the conversation from dispute to shared investigation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids both defensive escalation and premature capitulation
Proposes sharing concrete, independently verifiable evidence (example rows)
Shares the exact rule/definition used, addressing possible definitional mismatch
Frames the resolution as evidence-based collaboration, not a battle of confidence

questions.title: A Business Owner Refuses to Be Assigned as Term Steward
questions.prompt: You need a business owner assigned to a critical glossary term ('Customer Churn') so there's someone accountable for its definition. The VP you ask says, 'That's not really my job, just use whatever IT already has.' How do you handle this?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just accept 'use whatever IT already has,' because IT's existing calculation reflects a technical implementation decision someone made at some point, not necessarily a definition the business has actually validated as correct -- treating it as the governed answer by default skips the whole point of having a glossary at all. The right approach is explaining the actual stakes concretely: an unowned critical term means future disputes about what 'Customer Churn' really means have no accountable person to resolve them, and inconsistent reports built on different assumptions about it will eventually surface as a bigger, messier problem than a short definition review now. It also helps to reframe the ask as genuinely lightweight -- reviewing and approving a definition once, and being the point of contact if a dispute comes up later, not an ongoing operational burden. If the VP still won't own it after that, the right move is escalating to whoever runs data governance to get the term formally assigned an owner through the actual governance process, rather than leaving it ownerless because one VP declined.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just take 'use whatever IT has' as the answer, because that's not actually an ownership decision -- it's IT's technical implementation standing in for a business definition nobody has validated. I'd go back to the VP with something concrete rather than abstract governance language: 'if we don't have an owner for this, the next time Sales and Finance build competing Churn numbers, there's no one who can say which one is actually right -- that's going to cost more of your time later than five minutes now.' I'd also make clear what the ask actually is, because 'owner' can sound like a big commitment when it's really just reviewing a definition once and being the person people come to if there's a dispute later, not a new ongoing job. If that still doesn't land, I don't just quietly let the term stay unowned -- I'd take it to whoever actually runs data governance and ask them to assign it through the real process, because an unowned critical term isn't a problem I can solve by giving up after one no.
commonMistakes: Accepting IT's existing technical implementation as the governed definition by default, skipping real business validation
Giving up on getting an owner assigned after a single refusal instead of escalating through governance
Framing the ask as a large ongoing commitment instead of clarifying it's lightweight (review once, be the contact for disputes)
Not explaining the concrete future cost of leaving a critical term unowned
keyPoints: IT's existing implementation is not a substitute for a validated business definition and owner
Explaining the concrete future cost of an unowned critical term is more persuasive than abstract governance language
Reframing ownership as a lightweight, specific responsibility makes the ask easier to accept
If the business owner still declines, escalate through the actual governance process rather than leaving the term ownerless

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rejects 'use whatever IT has' as a substitute for validated business ownership
Makes a concrete, specific case for why an owner is needed
Reframes the ask as lightweight rather than a large ongoing burden
Escalates through governance if the direct ask still fails, rather than giving up

questions.title: Being Pressured to Approve an Urgent Change Without Full Impact Analysis
questions.prompt: You're asked to approve a schema change to a shared table. Your impact analysis shows 12 downstream reports are affected, but the requester says, 'This is urgent, just approve it, we don't have time for the full review.' How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't cave to the pressure and rubber-stamp the change, but it also doesn't just flatly refuse and leave it there -- it separates 'this is urgent' from 'this is exempt from any review at all,' which are two different claims. The practical move is proposing a faster, scoped version of the check instead of skipping it outright: identifying the highest-risk subset of the 12 affected reports and getting a quick go/no-go specifically from those owners, rather than doing the full 12-report review or doing nothing at all. If the situation is genuinely too time-critical even for that, the right response is presenting the real tradeoff explicitly to whoever actually has the authority to accept that risk, rather than silently absorbing the risk alone by approving it quietly. The point isn't rigid process adherence -- it's never letting urgency talk someone into skipping the analysis with nobody informed of the risk being taken.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just approve it because someone said it's urgent, and I also wouldn't hide behind 'policy says I need the full review' as my entire answer -- neither of those actually helps. What I'd do is offer a real alternative that respects the urgency without pretending the risk doesn't exist: 'I can get you an answer in an hour if we fast-track outreach to the 3 highest-risk report owners out of the 12 affected, instead of doing the full review on all twelve.' That's usually genuinely faster and still gives me something real to approve against, instead of nothing. If even that's too slow for whatever's driving the urgency, I'd say so explicitly and put the actual choice in front of whoever has the authority to accept that risk -- 'we can wait an hour for a partial check, or we go now and accept we might break something with zero warning, your call' -- rather than quietly approving it myself and hoping it works out, because that's me unilaterally accepting a risk that isn't really mine to accept alone.
commonMistakes: Approving the change immediately just because the requester framed it as urgent
Flatly refusing without offering any faster alternative, treating 'urgent' as irrelevant to the response
Silently approving under pressure and absorbing the risk alone instead of surfacing it to whoever has the authority to accept it
Not distinguishing a genuinely scoped, faster check from skipping the review entirely
keyPoints: Urgency is a reason to find a faster process, not a reason to skip analysis entirely
A scoped, faster check (highest-risk subset) is often a real, practical alternative to the full review
If truly time-critical, the risk tradeoff should be surfaced explicitly to whoever has authority to accept it
Never silently absorb the risk of skipping analysis alone just because pressure was applied

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids both reflexive approval under pressure and a rigid flat refusal
Proposes a concrete, faster scoped alternative to the full review
Surfaces the real risk tradeoff explicitly if a faster check still isn't possible
Never silently skips analysis or absorbs the risk alone

questions.title: A Steward Disagrees With the Automated Golden Record Decision
questions.prompt: The automated survivorship rule picked an address for a customer's golden record, but a data steward who knows the customer personally insists it's wrong and wants to override it. How do you handle this conflict between the automated rule and the steward's judgment?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't default to 'the automated system must be right because it's systematic,' and doesn't default to 'just let the steward override it because they know the customer,' either -- it treats the disagreement as a genuine signal worth investigating rather than deciding on authority alone. The right first step is checking which source and timestamp the surviving value actually came from, and verifying independently where possible, rather than simply taking either side's word for it. If the steward turns out to be right, there's a legitimate manual override/correction process that should be used -- and logged, so the correction is traceable and auditable, not a silent edit directly in the golden record table that leaves no trail. This situation is also worth treating as feedback on the survivorship rule itself: if this specific pattern (say, the 'most recent source' being stale for address specifically) keeps recurring, that's a signal the rule may need adjusting, not just a one-off correction every time it happens.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't automatically defer to the system just because it's systematic, and I wouldn't automatically defer to the steward just because they know the person, either -- I'd actually go look. The first thing I'd check is where the surviving address value came from and when it was last updated, because that tells me whether the rule did something reasonable given stale information, or whether something's actually wrong with the rule or the source data itself. If the steward's right, I wouldn't just go edit the golden record table directly -- that's exactly the kind of quiet, untracked change that makes a golden record untrustworthy over time. There's a proper correction process for exactly this, and it should leave a log of what changed, when, and why. And if I notice this isn't the first time this specific situation has come up -- survivorship consistently picking a stale value for address specifically -- I'd flag that as a signal the rule itself needs a second look, rather than treating every recurrence as its own isolated one-off fix.
commonMistakes: Automatically trusting the automated rule's output just because it's systematic rather than investigating
Automatically trusting the steward's personal knowledge without verifying against the actual source data
Editing the golden record directly instead of using a logged, traceable correction process
Treating a recurring version of this disagreement as a series of unrelated one-offs instead of a signal to review the rule
keyPoints: Neither the automated rule nor the steward's personal knowledge should be trusted by default without checking
Investigate the actual source and timestamp of the surviving value before deciding who's right
Corrections should go through a logged, traceable process, not a silent direct edit to the golden record
A recurring pattern of this disagreement is feedback that the survivorship rule itself may need adjusting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoids automatically deferring to either the rule or the steward without investigation
Describes concretely checking the source/timestamp of the surviving value
Requires a logged, traceable correction process rather than a silent edit
Recognizes a recurring pattern as feedback on the survivorship rule itself

questions.title: A VP Asks You to Bypass Masking 'Just This Once'
questions.prompt: A VP asks you to grant them temporary unmask access to a PII column they don't normally have access to, so they can personally debug a data issue, and says, 'just do it quietly, it's urgent and I don't want to go through the whole access request process.' How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer does not comply with 'quietly,' because an informal, unlogged access grant is exactly the kind of thing access governance and segregation of duties exist to prevent, regardless of how senior the person asking is -- seniority doesn't change what the control is protecting against. It also doesn't flatly refuse to help at all; the better move is offering to actually solve the underlying problem quickly through a legitimate path -- either fast-tracking the request through the real access process if an expedited option exists, or, often faster and safer, having someone who already holds legitimate access pull the specific unmasked data the VP needs to debug the issue, so the VP gets their answer without a new standing access grant ever being created. The response should briefly explain why the 'quietly' part specifically is the actual problem -- audit trail integrity, and the precedent it sets for the next senior person who asks for the same informal treatment -- rather than relitigating whether the VP has the authority to ask in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't do it quietly, full stop, regardless of who's asking -- that's not a judgment about the VP's intentions, it's that an unlogged access grant defeats the entire point of having access governance in the first place, and making an exception for seniority is exactly how that control erodes over time. But I also wouldn't just say no and leave them stuck, because the actual underlying need -- debugging a real issue, fast -- is legitimate and solvable without creating a new standing exception. I'd offer the faster real path: either push this through an expedited version of the actual access request if one exists, or, usually quicker, go to someone who already has legitimate unmask access and have them pull exactly the specific records needed to debug the issue, so the VP gets their answer today without anyone's access list growing by one more informal entry nobody will remember to revoke. I'd keep the explanation short and specific too -- it's not about doubting their need, it's that 'quietly' is the one word in the request I can't say yes to.
commonMistakes: Granting the informal, unlogged access because the requester is senior, treating seniority as an exception to governance
Flatly refusing to help at all instead of offering a legitimate faster path to the same outcome
Debating the VP's authority or intentions instead of focusing specifically on why 'quietly' is the problem
Not offering a concrete alternative (expedited request, or someone with existing access pulling the specific data)
keyPoints: An informal, unlogged access grant should never be made regardless of the requester's seniority
The response should still solve the real underlying need quickly through a legitimate path
Having someone with existing legitimate access pull the specific data needed is often the fastest safe alternative
The explanation should focus specifically on why 'quietly' is the issue, not the requester's authority to ask

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Firmly declines the informal/unlogged request regardless of seniority
Offers a concrete, legitimate faster alternative rather than a flat refusal
Explains specifically why the informal/unlogged nature is the actual problem
Response stays professional and solution-focused rather than adversarial

questions.title: Stakeholders Say the Catalog Is Full of Noise and Nobody Uses It
questions.prompt: Six months after rolling out Microsoft Purview, business users complain the data catalog is cluttered with poorly described, uncurated assets and they've stopped trying to use it. How do you respond, and what would you actually do to fix adoption?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't dismiss the complaint or respond with 'search harder' -- low adoption driven by clutter is a real and common governance failure mode: scanning a source without curating what gets discovered just produces a pile of raw technical metadata, not a usable catalog, and users correctly stop trusting a tool that mostly returns noise. The concrete fix starts with prioritization rather than trying to perfect everything at once: identify a smaller set of genuinely high-value, frequently-needed assets -- critical data elements, the reports people actually ask about most -- and curate those first with real descriptions, owners, and glossary links, rather than spreading thin curation effort evenly across everything that was scanned. Assign actual owners responsible for those priority assets' descriptions with a real deadline, consider deprioritizing or hiding clearly low-value scanned noise from default search results, and re-survey the same users once the curated subset improves -- treating adoption as something to measure and iterate on, not a one-time rollout event that either succeeded or failed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't tell them to just search better, because the complaint is legitimate -- if scanning ran without any real curation behind it, the catalog is mostly a pile of raw schema with no descriptions or owners, and of course people stopped trying to use something that mostly returns noise. What I'd actually do is stop trying to fix the whole catalog at once and pick a genuinely small, high-value slice first -- the handful of critical data elements and reports people actually ask about constantly -- and get those properly curated with real descriptions, named owners, and glossary links, rather than spreading effort evenly across thousands of scanned assets that mostly nobody needs. I'd assign specific people to that priority list with an actual deadline, and I'd also just hide or deprioritize the obviously low-value noise from what shows up by default in search, so what people see first is the curated part, not the raw pile. Then I'd go back to the same users who complained once that's done and ask again -- adoption isn't something you declare finished at rollout, it's something you have to keep checking and fixing.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the complaint or suggesting users just need to search more effectively
Trying to curate every scanned asset evenly instead of prioritizing a smaller high-value subset first
Not assigning actual owners with deadlines for the priority curation work
Treating the initial rollout as finished instead of re-measuring adoption after improvements are made
keyPoints: Low adoption from clutter is a real, common failure mode: scanning without curation produces noise, not a usable catalog
Prioritizing a smaller set of high-value assets for real curation is more effective than spreading effort evenly
Assigning owners with deadlines, and deprioritizing low-value noise from default search, are concrete fixes
Adoption should be re-measured after improvements, treated as ongoing, not a one-time rollout event

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Takes the complaint seriously and correctly diagnoses scanning-without-curation as the cause
Proposes prioritizing a smaller high-value subset for curation rather than everything at once
Proposes concrete ownership/deadline and noise-reduction actions
Treats adoption as something to re-measure and iterate on, not a one-time event
